ergo et plures unctiones sunt unum sacramentum. / Ad hoc si non esset unum sacramenti sic facta prima unctione non oporteret ad perfectionem sacramenti quod fieret secunda. quia quilibet sacramentum per se habet esse perfectum. sed hoc falsum est. ergo est unum sacramentum.
Ulterius videtur quod hoc sacramentum non fuit institutum a christo. quia de institutione sacramentorum que christus instituit fit mentio in euangelio sicut de eucharistia et baptismo. sed nulla fit mentio de extrema unctione. ergo non est a christo instituta. / Ad magister expresse dicit in littera quod est institutum ab apostolis. ergo ipse christus per se non instituit. /
Preterea a euiusdem est statuere sacramentum eucharistie quod christus instituit: etiam ipse per se exhibuit. sed hoc sacramentum ipse nulli exhibuit. ergo per se non instituit. / Sed contra sacramenta noue legis sunt digniora quam sacramenta veteris legis. sed omnia sacramenta noue legis sunt ab ipso deo instituta. ergo multo fortius omnia sacramenta noue legis habent institutionem ab hominibus apostolorum habet eandem auctoritatem quam apostoli habuerunt. non posset auferre sacramentum extreme unctionis. ergo apostoli non instituerunt sed ipse christus.
Respondeo dicendum ad primam questionem in his que ecclesia visibiliter operatur quedam sunt sacramenta. ut baptismus. quedam sacramentalia. ut exorcisimus. ut supra di. vi. dictum est. quorum hec est differentia. quia sacramentum dicitur illa actio ecce quod attingit ad effectum principaliter intentum in administratione sacramentorum. sed sacramentalia dicitur illa actio que quamuis non perangat ad illam actionem principalem effectum. autem intentus in administratione aliquo modo ad illam actionem principalem effectum. aut est auferre morbi peccati. ipsa per vi. hoc est o ut verbis iacobi patet. nec ordinetur ad aliud hunc effectum pertingat extrema unctio. ut sacramentum quasi et annexum. constat quod ad baptismum non est sacramentale sed sacramentum. / Ad primum ergo dicendum quod oleum quo cathecumini unguntur sua unctione non perducit ad peccati remissionem. quia hi ad baptismum pertinet sed aliquo modo ad baptismum disponit. ut supra di. vi. dictum est. et ideo non est sacram illa unctio sic unctio extrema.
Ad secundum quod sacramentum immediate

hominem ad gloriam disponit ad exeuntibus. a corpore detur. et quia in veteri lege non erat adhuc tempus perueniendi ad gloriam. quia neminem ad gloriam adduxit lex. ideo istud sacramentum ibi prefigurari non debuit per aliquis aliquo modo figuratum sit in omnibus aurati omnibus que leguntur in veteri testamento. /
Ad tertium dicendum quod dyonisius non facit aliquam mentionem de extrema unctione. siue aut nec de penitentia nec de matrimonio. quia ipse non intendit determinare de sacramentis nisi quatenus per ea innotescere potest ecclesiastice ierarchie ordinata disposio quantu ad ministros et actiones ministrorum et recipientes. tamen cum per extremam unctionem aliquis consequatur gratiam et remissione peccatorum non est dubium quod habet vim illuminatiuam et purgatiuam sicut baptismus quamuis non ita plenam. Ad h. questionem dicen dum quod unum numero per se loquendo diatur tripliater. uno modo sicut indiuisibile. quod nec actu nec potencia est plura. ut punctus et vnitas. Alio modo sicut continuu quod quidez est unum actu sed plura potencia. ut linea. Sed verao modo fiat perfectum aliquod quod ex pluribus partibus constituitur. ut domus. quod est multa quodammodo etiam actu sed illa multa conueniunt in aliquo uno. et hoc modo quotlibet sacramentum dicitur unum. in quantum multa que sunt de uno sacramento adunantur ad unum signandum vel causandum qua sacramentum signando causat. et ideo in vna actio suffiat ad perfectam significationem. vnitas sacramenti consistit in illa actione tantum. sicut patet in confirmatione. in vna et in multis actionibus tunc sacramentum per se potest et vna actione et pluribus. sicut ablutio que significatur in baptismo. po test esse per vnam immersionem. vel per multas. quando autem perfecta significatio non potest esse nisi per plures actiones. tunc plures actiones sunt de perfectione sacramenti. sicut patet de eucharistia. quia refecto corpora lis quidem significat spiritualem refectio non potest esse nisi per abum et per potum. et similiter etiam est in hoc sacramento. quia non test perfecte significari nisi tantum per appositionem mediane ad diuersas vulnerum

23.

Therefore, many anointings are one sacrament. To this, if it were not one sacrament, it would not be necessary, the first anointing having been done, that a second be performed for the perfection of the sacrament, because every sacrament of itself must have a perfect being. But this is false; therefore, it is one sacrament.

Furthermore, it seems that this sacrament was not instituted by Christ, because mention is made in the Gospel concerning the institution of the sacraments that Christ instituted, such as the Eucharist and baptism; but no mention is made concerning extreme unction; therefore, it is not instituted by Christ. The Master <note>Peter Lombard</note> expressly says in the text that it is instituted by the Apostles; therefore, Christ himself did not institute it personally.

Moreover, it belongs to the same authority to establish the sacrament of the Eucharist, which Christ instituted and also exhibited personally. But this sacrament, he exhibited to no one; therefore, he did not institute it personally. But on the contrary, the sacraments of the New Law are more worthy than the sacraments of the Old Law; but all the sacraments of the New Law are instituted by God himself; therefore, much more strongly, all the sacraments of the New Law have institution. [Regarding the argument] that the Apostles have the same authority that the Apostles had, he could not remove the sacrament of extreme unction; therefore, the Apostles did not institute it, but Christ himself did.

I answer that it must be said to the first question: in those things which the Church visibly performs, some are sacraments, as baptism; some are sacramentals, as exorcism, as was said above in distinction 6. Of these, this is the difference: a sacrament is called that action of the Church which reaches the effect primarily intended in the administration of the sacraments. But a sacramental is called that action which, although it does not attain to that principal effect, is intended in the administration in some way towards that principal effect, or is to remove the disease of sin. This is clear by the words of James <note>James 5:15</note>; nor is it ordered to another end but reaches this effect, extreme unction, as if annexed to the sacrament. It is evident that it is not a sacramental, but a sacrament.

To the first, therefore, it must be said that the oil with which catechumens are anointed does not, by its anointing, lead to the remission of sin, because they pertain to baptism, but it disposes in some way to baptism, as was said above in distinction 6, and therefore that anointing is not a sacrament, as is extreme anointing.

To the second, that the sacrament immediately disposes a man for glory, for those departing from the body. And because in the Old Law there was not yet the time for arriving at glory, because the law led no one to glory, therefore this sacrament should not be prefigured there, although it is in some way figured in all things that are read in the Old Testament.

To the third, it must be said that Dionysius does not make any mention of extreme unction, nor of penance, nor of matrimony, because he does not intend to determine concerning the sacraments except insofar as the ordered disposition of the ecclesiastical hierarchy can be known through them regarding ministers, the actions of ministers, and the recipients. Nevertheless, since through extreme unction one attains grace and the remission of sins, there is no doubt that it has illuminating and purging power, like baptism, although not as full.

To this question, it must be said that "one in number," speaking for itself, is said in three ways. In one way, as indivisible, which is not many either actually or potentially, like a point and unity. In another way, as continuous, which is indeed one actually but many potentially, like a line. In the third way, a perfect thing is made which is constituted from many parts, like a house, which is many in a way even actually, but those many come together in one thing. And in this way, any sacrament is called one, insofar as many things which are of one sacrament are gathered to signify or cause one thing, since the sacrament causes by signifying. And therefore, one action suffices for perfect signification; the unity of the sacrament consists in that action alone, as is evident in confirmation. In one and many actions, the sacrament can be per se both by one action and by many, just as the ablution which is signified in baptism can be by one immersion or by many. However, when a perfect signification cannot be, except through many actions, then many actions are of the perfection of the sacrament, as is evident concerning the Eucharist, because corporeal refaction indeed signifies spiritual refaction, which cannot be except through bread and wine. And similarly, it is also in this sacrament, because it cannot be perfectly signified except only through the application of the medicine to the different <note>parts of the body, signifying the</note> wounds.

<summary>This page clarifies the definition of a sacrament versus a sacramental, rejects the idea that extreme unction is merely a preparatory ritual, and explains the nature of sacramental unity through the analogy of parts forming a whole.</summary>

<margin>Regarding monks who transfer to other orders. If any monk wishes to move from one monastery to another, he must not do this without the license of his abbot. And if he has moved, he must be recalled to his own monastery.</margin>

<note>A blue and red flourished initial 'P' begins the first block of text.</note>

After he has been neither received by him, nor acquired by the monks or the place, nor alienated by others in any way, even by the grace of the Lord, let those who commit this manifest error be corrected for their sins by the mediator of all. Regarding the others, as much as you can, and regarding the office of hearing confession or burial, let this be applied to those judged or to those in unwilling orders, and from those who have obtained the same while unwilling, and since it has proceeded, we do not in the least forbid the execution of the present constitution. We also decide that those of the order of hermits or of the Augustinians who attempt to receive [anything] in any way, notwithstanding, shall be subject to the present [ruling] through friendship. To the promised orders to which [this] against the present [ruling] extends, we also generally grant to other approved orders that no one at all may be led to another, nor may they and their places be released from the permission of the same holy see regarding these matters, nothing notwithstanding.

<note>A red and blue flourished initial 'P' begins the second block of text.</note>

We also command that bishops should not invite monks or nuns, nor should they come from those from whom it is not customary, so that the statute of the council notwithstanding, they should not be removed unless for a reasonable cause. Regarding the reception of persons. No layman, unless by the right of the church competent to him, may confer this same or another church to a religious place, nor should such [a person] do this unless by the consent of the same [bishop] it can be effectively shown; through the aforementioned, unless the bishop who could not give assent to the same, unless he detects malice. No layman should have the right to present [someone] to an office.

<column-break/>

<note>A blue and red flourished initial 'R' begins the right column.</note>

The Roman Church, which extends its authority to all parts of the world and wishes to judge over those who persuade it, through its charity, cares more and provides for the opportunity to visit fully; nor is it said to be friendly only towards the greater but also the lesser, and it intends for the same visitation if it knows that one cannot access any of them without difficulty; it should strive to convoke from many to one suitable [place] those from the neighbors and laymen, lest it remit in the petition of the visitation, and throughout the province, caring to execute its part in the office of visitation, it also [commands] its suffragans and their subjects to this kind of grace, even broad grace, to both religious and pious places, to the clergy and the people themselves, so that they may be prepared to administer; whatever [arises] by right of visitation (even if one of them is visited by the diocesan visitation chapter afterwards, the visitation may pulse to that, and all remaining dioceses of the same province can be visited in whole or in part or separately), to those by whom the visitation was conducted, also if he visits in the same diocese where there is more need of visitation than others, before other visitations, [the bishop] may return to the same [place] as requested by the diocesan statute, so that if he comes, he may at least feed the greater ones, with the council and craft of the bishop of the same province applied.

<margin>Note that a layman cannot confer a church without the authority of the bishop.</margin>

<note>A red flourished initial 'V' marks the bottom of the right column.</note>

<summary>This page addresses the regulations regarding monastic transfers, the limitations on lay involvement in church appointments, and the procedural authority of the Roman Church in conducting visitations.</summary>

In controuersia, Utrum arte Chymica possit naturaliter fieri transmutatio rerum viliorum in pretiosiores, adeoque utrum effici possit aurum ex viliori Metallo, videtur afferendum, Nulla efficaci ratione ostendi posse confectionem auri omnino impossibilem esse (tametsi perdifficilis indue-tur/siquidem ea nec repugnat ex parte materiæ, quæ idonea est alterari & perduci ad formam auri, nec ex parte modi, qui est per naturalem decoctionem ignis, quamuis enim plura fortè, quàm humana industria suppleri queant, requirantur, vt ex terra & aqua, seu exhalatione & vapore primú corpus mixtum existat & coaguletur, ideoque auri substantia ex terræ puluere, & aquæ liquore in venis Cauernarum solo calore perfici nequeat, sed frigiditas quo-que & siccitas requirantur; Attamen pauciora exiguntur, vt ex mixto iam coagulato & existante aliud conficiatur mixtum perfectione differens; ac proinde vbi metallum iam coaluit in substantiam metalli, solus ignis poterit supplere quæ ad perficiendum & commutandum illud metallum in alterum erunt necessaria: quod maximè verum est si metalla non differunt specie, vt ex Callisthene docet Alb. Mag. lib. 3. de metallis tr. 1. c. 7.

LIV. Itaque longè probabilius videtur posse Alchimiam finem suum consequi, & alia metalla in aurum igne transmutare, quàm non posse: cum enim artis humanæ industria possint animalia quædam ex corporibus inanimis, vt ex ventribus mactatorum boum recentibus, fimo tantum obrutis, apes generari, cur non etiam metalla (quæ vniuersim loquendo inanimata sunt) præstantiora ex vilioribus gigni queant? præsertim cum vilioribus metallis credatur inesse quoddam veluti semen auri, eis naturaliter, hoc est, ratione naturæ suæ genericæ aut specificæ, insitum, quod semen à cælorum influxu quodammodò impressum, calore fouetur & adolescit in aurum. Porrò etsi nullo iure in foro fori, ars producendi aurum videatur esse prohibita, vt non liceat eam passim exercere, nihilominus tamen saltem ratione circumstantiarum, hoc est, finis, modi, personæ ac temporis merito illicitam & perniciosam iudicat. Gregor. de Valent. tom. 3. disp. 6. q. 13. p. 2. & consentit Delr. in fine 1. lib. cum ait, In foro poli non promiscue, sed cum delectu eam permittendam, immò plerisque vt perniciosam, sic & illicitam censendam.

LIII. In the controversy regarding whether the transmutation of baser things into more precious ones can occur naturally through the art of alchemy, and therefore whether gold can be made from a baser metal, it seems one must argue that there is no effective reason to show the production of gold is entirely impossible. Although it is considered extremely difficult, it is not repugnant in terms of matter, which is suitable to be altered and led to the form of gold, nor in terms of method, which is through the natural cooking <note>original: "decoctionem"</note> of fire. Although perhaps more things are required than human industry can supply so that a mixed body might exist and coagulate from earth and water, or from exhalation and vapor—and therefore the substance of gold cannot be perfected in the veins of caverns from the dust of the earth and the liquid of water solely by heat, but cold and dryness are also required—nevertheless, fewer things are required to produce another mixture differing in perfection from a mixture that has already coagulated and exists. Consequently, where a metal has already coalesced into the substance of a metal, fire alone will be able to supply what is necessary to perfect and change that metal into another. This is most true if the metals do not differ in species, as Albertus Magnus teaches in Book 3, On Metals, tractate 1, chapter 7, following Callisthenes.

LIV. Therefore, it seems far more probable that alchemy can achieve its goal and transmute other metals into gold by fire than that it cannot. For since, by the industry of human art, certain animals can be generated from inanimate bodies, such as bees from the fresh bellies of slaughtered oxen buried only in dung, why can more excellent metals (which are, generally speaking, inanimate) not also be produced from baser ones? Especially since it is believed that a certain seed, as it were, of gold resides within baser metals, implanted in them naturally—that is, by reason of their generic or specific nature—which seed, having been in some way impressed by the influx of the heavens, is nurtured by heat and grows into gold. Furthermore, although the art of producing gold does not seem to be prohibited by any law in the public forum, such that it is not permitted to practice it here and there, nevertheless, it is deservedly judged illicit and pernicious at least by reason of the circumstances; that is, the end, the manner, the person, and the time. Gregory of Valencia, volume 3, disputation 6, question 13, part 2, and Delrio agrees at the end of book 1 when he says that in the forum of the conscience <note>original: "in foro poli"</note> it should not be permitted indiscriminately, but with discretion; indeed, for most people, it should be considered as pernicious as it is illicit.

ferentia et distinctiones, quomodo ausus es dicere, tuam
benedictionem sumpsisse eum, qui nullam illius modi
tui partem accepit?

Quare interrogatus, tantane non est reservata mihi
benedictio, pater respondit: Si dominum tuum illum
constitui et omnes fratres eius famulos feci, areis
arboribusque firmavi eum, tibi ergo qui in iram
me movisti, quid faciam, fili **)?

§. 230. Virtute (sive in intellectu) ait, nec unum
ex votis orationis, quae conveniebat (tibi) nunc col-
ligere et acquirere ut bonum proprium, reservavi tibi.
Quoniam ex ipsa natura bonus est princeps, dominus
et dives; insipiens autem pauper, servus, inops. Ve-
rum convenit inquirere, quosnam fratres dicit Iacob
fuisse, quum unicus sit et gemellus. Sed videtur
in allegoriam nos revocare et fere manifeste vocat;
non enim de hominibus est interim sermo eius, sed
de symbolis animarum, quae secundum singulas par-
tes irrationales conflantur, secundum nimirum visum <margin>P. A 429</margin>
et auditum, gustum, odoratum, tactum, adde affectus
inclinationesque et cupiditates, timoremque et tristitiam;
nam haec omnia affines sunt animae et fratres. Cete-
rum quando filium eum dicit, non sicut de filio te-
statur ei prognationem (consortium filiationis) ***), sed
sicut puero ruditatem.

---

*) Ad verbum: o iste vel talis, ὦ οὗτος. Auch. **) Genes.
27, 36. 37. ***) Vel comprolitatem, si ita dici queat
Latine, ut dicitur Arm. ut Gr. συγγονεία, etc. Auch.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 27, specifically analyzing Esau's accusations against Jacob and the allegorical nature of their brotherhood.</meta>

PHIL.IUD.QUAEST.IN GEN.L.IV. §. 229. 230.

He is proven guilty of a lie, for he said: "And now he has stolen my blessing." To which anyone might rightly reply: He did not take your blessing, O (foolish) man <note>original: "ὦ οὗτος"</note>, but one suitable for himself. For your blessing had its beginning from the earth, but his truly from heaven. You were inscribed among the servants, he among the masters. For you, the hope is the sword and war; but for him, peace is lovable, and he himself is a man of peace <note>original: "pacificus"</note>. Since, therefore, there are so many and such great differences and distinctions, how did you dare to say that he, who received no part of such a thing as yours, has taken your blessing?

Why, when asked if there was not a blessing reserved for him, did the father answer: "If I have made him your lord, and have made all his brothers his servants, and have confirmed him with grain and wine, what then shall I do for you, my son?" <note>original: "Genesis 27:36, 37"</note>

§. 230. By "virtue" (or in the intellect) he says that he has not reserved for you even one of the vows of prayer, which it was fitting (for you) now to gather and acquire as a proper good. Since by nature itself the prince, lord, and rich man is good; but the foolish man is poor, a servant, and needy. Yet it is appropriate to inquire which brothers he says Jacob had, when he is unique and a twin. But he seems to call us back to allegory and almost explicitly names it. For his discourse is not meanwhile about men, but about symbols of souls, which are formed according to individual irrational parts, namely according to sight and hearing, taste, smell, touch, and add to these the affections, inclinations, and desires, as well as fear and sadness; for all these are related to the soul and are its brothers. Furthermore, when he calls him "son," he does not testify to his lineage (consortium of filiation) <note>original: "συγγένεια"</note>, but as to a child, his immaturity.

<margin>P. A 428</margin>
<margin>P. A 429</margin>

<summary>Philo analyzes Esau's false claim that Jacob stole his blessing, contrasting the earthly, combative nature of Esau with the heavenly, peaceful nature of Jacob. He further interprets the "brothers" and "son" mentioned in the text not as physical individuals, but as allegorical representations of the irrational parts of the soul and the immaturity of the foolish mind.</summary>

# TRACTATVS DE AQVIS MINERALIBVS
## PARS SECVNDA.

### CAPVT. I.
### Segregationis aquarum apparatus.

<margin>A</margin> QVA ipsa vel tota in se consideratur, vel in compositionis membra segregata, quorum deinceps vnum quodque pro se spectatur. Vtrobique communia sunt multa. Examinabimus primum ea quae sensibus sunt propiora; postea quae magis sunt rationis, hoc est effecta: quibus praemittemus separationis modos, qui huic rei solent accommodari.

Vt itaque per segregationes perueniamus ad notitiam partium compositionis: Est enim omnis aqua mineralis ex genere imperfecte mistorum: haurienda ab ipso fonte est certa quantitas, quo tempore maximè est sui, valet virtute, liberaque est a turbis elementaribus, ab iniuria animalium, áque similibus externis; quod fieri posse iudicant tempore sereno diutius, ante autumnum paulo, sub auroram, cum quieuerit satis ab haurientibus, potantibusue, cum venti non bacchantur &c. estque instituenda segregatio non procul a fonte, ne dum longius effertur spirituum quorumdam iacturam capiat. Vasa sint vitrea, aut lapidea, impenetrabilia halitibus, aut succis mordacibus, nisi cum examinis ratio requirit aut permittit etiam metallica, lignea, figulina fara, &c.

### CAP. II.
### Segregatio spirituum.

<margin>A</margin> Quae pondus certum statim mittatur in cucurbitam cum alembico, cuius rostrum transeat per refrigeria, aut ipse instratus sit refrigeratoriis pannis, &c. Apponatur excipulus, tenaciq; maltha commissurae omnes obstruantur quam exactissimè. Cucurbita in fimo leni, vel balneo vaporis, aut saltem maris tepido locetur, vt abstrahantur spiritus subtilissimi. Hi examinentur sigillatim, sicut & aqua in cucurbita relicta. Postea comparentur, vt constet in quanam parte virtus sit potior. Potest & vtraque ad pondus reuocari. Quod si nulli aut paucissimi prolecti fuerint, corpulentam potius misturam esse, aut, si mauis, spiritus terrestriores tanquam succos resolutos in liquore arbitrandum est.

### CAP. III.
### Aquositatis segregatio & contentorum.

<margin>S</margin> Ed siue aliquid prodierit, siue nihil, transferatur vas in cineres, & prouocetur pars aquosa vsque ad consistentiam melleam, si talis fore iudicabitur. Partes spectentur item seorsim, & postea inter se conferantur. Quod residuum est, perfundatur aliqua parte extractae aquae (si quidem iudicabitur aliqua crassa consistentia) & immaceretur. Postea transfundatur. Transfusum coaguletur vsque ad spissitudinem eam quae est lixiuiorum, aluminis, & similium succorum. Tunc immittantur in vtramque partem vel culmi, vel funiculi, vel bacilli, &c. Et expectetur coagulatio, vel etiam in vitrea concha paulatim tepore fornacis clauso vase fiat diuaporatio. Contenta erunt in fundo. Si nulla apparet spissitudo postquam exhausta maior pars subtilitatis est, ponatur ad putrescendum per mensem. Si ne tunc quidem hypostasis inuenitur, destilletur, vel diuaporatur prorsus. Vbi enim nulla fit secessio, nec inueniuntur reliquae, spiritalis tota est contemperatio, aestimabiturque virtus, & natura ex destillato & residuo per collationem mutuam. Notabis autem ubi per lenissimum calorem tenuissimos spiritus segregasti, in secunda destillatione cinerum mutato receptaculo, eoque mobili relicto inter destillandum crebrius guttas esse contemplandas, gustandasque. Si enim resipiunt eandem vim mineralem, aut nouam exhibent, aut etiam, vt aqua, sunt insipidae, rationem separationis exactius poteris determinare, & diuersos liquores diuersis vasis excipere. Etiam oculis notare licet, quando spiritus inuisibiles desinunt succedentibus aqueis. Tunc enim sudat alembicus, & riuulis distinguitur. Hac sola ratione si solerter egeris, poteris potissimas partes elicere. Nam prima operatio spiritus praebet, secunda aquas corpulentiores seu minerales, seu insipidas purasque. Tertia separat succos concretiles a calcibus, quin & alumen ab attramento, salem ab halinitro, &c.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the effects of mineral waters on external objects to a systematic laboratory analysis of the water’s internal components through distillation and evaporation.</meta>

On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.

# A TREATISE ON MINERAL WATERS
## PART TWO.

### CHAPTER I.
### The apparatus for the separation of waters.

<margin>A</margin> Water itself is considered either as a whole in itself, or as separated into its component parts, each of which is then viewed on its own. In both cases, many things are held in common. We will first examine those things which are closer to the senses; then those which belong more to reason, that is, the effects: before which we will place the methods of separation that are usually adapted to this matter.

So that we may arrive at a knowledge of the component parts through separation—for every mineral water is of the category of "imperfect mixtures"—a certain quantity must be drawn from the spring itself at the time when it is most truly itself, strong in its power, and free from elemental disturbances, from the harm caused by animals, and from similar external factors. This is judged to be possible during a long period of clear weather, shortly before autumn, at dawn, when the spring has rested enough from those drawing or drinking it, and when the winds are not raging, etc. The separation should be established not far from the spring, lest it suffer a loss of certain spirits <term>spirituum<gloss>volatile components or essences</gloss></term> while being carried further away. The vessels should be of glass or stone, impenetrable to vapors or corrosive juices, unless the nature of the examination requires or even permits metallic, wooden, or earthenware <term>figulina fara<gloss>pottery vessels</gloss></term> ones, etc.

### CHAPTER II.
### The separation of spirits.

<margin>A</margin> Once a certain weight has been measured, let it be immediately put into a cucurbit <term>cucurbitam<gloss>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</gloss></term> with an alembic <term>alembico<gloss>the cap or head of a still</gloss></term>, whose beak should pass through cooling systems, or let it be covered with cooling cloths, etc. Let a receiver <term>excipulus<gloss>a vessel to catch the distillate</gloss></term> be attached, and let all the joints be blocked as precisely as possible with tenacious mastic <term>maltha<gloss>a cement or putty used to seal laboratory equipment</gloss></term>. Let the cucurbit be placed in gentle dung <note>Dung was used as a source of low, steady heat for "digesting" substances.</note>, or a vapor bath, or at least a lukewarm water bath <term>balneo maris<gloss>literally a "bath of the sea"; a bain-marie</gloss></term>, so that the most subtle spirits may be drawn off. Let these be examined one by one, as well as the water left in the cucurbit. Afterward, let them be compared, so that it may be clear in which part the power is more potent. Both can also be reduced to their weight. But if none or very few are drawn out, it must be judged that the mixture is rather "corpulent" <note>Thick or heavy</note>, or, if you prefer, that the spirits are more earthy, like juices dissolved in the liquid.

### CHAPTER III.
### Separation of the wateriness and the contents.

<margin>S</margin> But whether something has come forth or nothing, let the vessel be transferred to the ashes <note>A sand or ash bath allows for higher heat than a water bath.</note>, and let the watery part be provoked until it reaches a honey-like consistency, if such is judged to be appropriate. Let the parts be viewed separately likewise, and then compared with one another. What remains should be drenched with some part of the extracted water (if indeed a certain thick consistency is judged) and allowed to soak. Afterward, let it be poured off. Let the poured-off liquid be coagulated to the thickness of lye, alum, and similar juices. Then let either straws, or small cords, or little rods, etc., be placed into both parts. And let coagulation be expected, or else let evaporation <term>diuaporatio<gloss>slow evaporation by heat</gloss></term> occur in a glass shell gradually by the heat of the furnace in a closed vessel. The contents will be at the bottom. If no thickness appears after the greater part of the subtle matter has been exhausted, let it be set to "putrefy" <note>In early chemistry, this refers to a slow digestion or fermentation process, not necessarily rotting.</note> for a month. If even then no sediment <term>hypostasis<gloss>a deposit or sediment</gloss></term> is found, let it be distilled or evaporated entirely. For where no separation occurs and no remains are found, the entire mixture is of a spiritual nature, and its power and nature will be estimated from the distillate and the residue through mutual comparison. Note, however, that where you have separated the thinnest spirits by the gentlest heat, in the second distillation over ashes, with the receiver changed and kept movable during the distillation, the drops should be observed and tasted more frequently. For if they taste of the same mineral power, or exhibit a new one, or are even tasteless like water, you will be able to determine the method of separation more exactly, and receive different liquids in different vessels. It is also possible to note by sight when the invisible spirits cease and are succeeded by watery ones. For then the alembic "sweats" and is marked by little streams. By this method alone, if you act skillfully, you will be able to draw out the most essential parts. For the first operation provides the spirits; the second, the heavier waters, whether mineral or tasteless and pure. The third separates the solidifiable juices from the "limes" <term>calcibus<gloss>residues left after calcination or evaporation</gloss></term>, and indeed alum from vitriol <term>attramento<gloss>literally "ink," often used for vitriol or copperas</gloss></term>, salt from niter <term>halinitro<gloss>a natural saltpeter or soda</gloss></term>, etc.

<summary>This page describes the laboratory procedures for analyzing mineral water by separating its volatile "spirits" from its watery and solid components using distillation and evaporation. It details the equipment needed, such as cucurbits and alembics, and the specific temperatures required for each stage of analysis.</summary>

translation: is known. However, I had never experienced in it what I am about to say. Indeed, with a stylus which one of those men happened to have, he struck the middle of the animal. Then both parts of the body moved away from that wound. With such speed of feet and no less diligent effort, as if they were two living beings. Terrified by this miracle, and curious about the cause, we went to the place where I and other pious men were sitting together, and we brought out those pieces which were living vigorously. We were not slightly moved, and we observed them running on the table in whatever direction they could. And if one touched them with a stylus, it would twist itself toward the place of pain, while the other felt nothing and went about its own movements elsewhere. Why say more? We tested how much value this had, and we cut the little worm, or rather, now the little worms, into many parts. They all moved in such a way that, if that had not been done by us and the wounds were not fresh, I would have believed that they had been born whole and separate and had lived each for its own sake. But what I said to those young men then, as they looked at me intently, I fear to say to you now. For we have already proceeded so far that, unless you have something that carries weight for my cause, our great effort, reinforced by such a long discourse, might succumb, having been pierced by a single little worm. I commanded them, however, to keep to their course in their studies just as they had begun, so that they might acquire and learn these things when the opportunity serves, if the matter demands it. But what I discussed with Alipius as they departed, which each of us, according to his own measure, ought to remember, contemplate, and inquire into, if you wish me to explain it, must be said to you at greater length, since it was stated from the very beginning with such mazes and windings. I will not, however, keep silent before you about what I sense, unless many things were already known to me then about the body, about the form that is within the body, about place and time, about motion, which those who say the soul is a body discuss most subtly and abstrusely in order to give the palm to their own side, which I must deflect. For this reason, I warn you again and again, as best I can, not to be rashly swayed either by books or by the disputes of very talkative men who are too excessively attached to the sense of these bodies.

### Dracunculus. Cap. XCVI

<margin>D</margin>Racunculus maior, ut Dioscorides testatum reliquit, prouenit in opacis & circum septa, caule glabro læuiq́, recto, bicubitali, baculi crassamento, uersicoloribus draconum maculis, euincentibus numero purpureis, folijs rumicis, mutuo complexu aduersis. Fructū summo caule facit racemosum, coloris inter initia cineracei, postea quàm ematuruit, croceo & puniceo rutilantis, radice grandi, candida, rotunda, tenui cortice tunicata. Carpitur cum nigrescit maturitate. Sed hæc supposititia mihi uidetur, præsertim cum & Galenus, & Paulus, qui huius authoris dicta bona fide solent referre, unius tantum dracunculi meminerint. Auxit quoque suspicionem, quòd huius picturæ apud ueteres, qui Dioscoridis ubique placitis adhæserunt, nullum uestigium ostenditur: & si ueterrima quæque consulantur exemplaria, comperientur tandem nihil minoris maiorisq́ dracūculi discrimine notasse. Sed uter minor dicetur, cum cauli utriusq́ bicubitalis assignetur altitudo? Quare caput quod maiori dracunculo dicatum est, historiæ Dioscoridis accreuisse suspicamur, præsertim cum uterque faciem eandem, magnitudinem, habitum, uersicoloriam cutem, natales eosdem sibi uendicauit. Nam uterque in umbrosis circum sepes & senticeta nascitur, rotunda radice, tenui libro uestita, caule recto, bicubitali, baculi crassitudine, uersicoloribus anguium maculis, intercursantibus lituris purpureis, fructu in cacumine racemoso, primum acinis in pallore uirentibus. quare in altero cineraceo, in altero herbaceo legitur. qui cum ematuruerunt, croci colore uel punico rutilant. Sed quod lectorem potissimum male haberet, est, quòd folijs uidentur multum discrepare, in altero rumicis, in altero hederacea designantur. Sed in longè distantiores angulos exeunt, nec legitimo hederæ circino rotundātur. Huius folij faciem Dioscorides explicuit, in hemionij mentione. nam hemionium dracunculi folio repræsentauit, quod prælongum est, & ferè rumicis figura. Hinc uulgus nostrum sua consuetudine linguam cerui uocat hemionium. Quare ut omnis facessat suspicio, unum genus tantum dracūculi credimus, historia duplici repræsentatum, priorem tamen adiectitiam fuisse, nec ex Dioscoridis sed alterius authoris officina prodijsse iudicamus. Adde, quòd uires, & si uarijs uocibus enarrentur, non tamen dissimiles multum aut abhorrentes à sese comperiuntur. In orbe nostro satis frequens inuenitur, & in hortis studiose colitur, ludentis naturæ miraculū, & draconis rudimenta in stirpibus facere condiscentis. Simplici caule dracunculus attollitur, binum cubitum alto, læui, glabroq́, baculi crassitudine, uersicoloribus anguium maculis uariegato, purpureis etiā intercursantibus lituris, ita ut plane serpentis habitum coloremq́ mentiri uideatur. In uertice comoso folia prodeunt, sena septena'ue, crassiore pediculo digitorum ritu propendentia, candicantibus respersa notis, rumicis figura, specie tamē hederacea longiore. E foliato scapi fastigio uagina quædam foris herbacea prosilit, cubitalis ferè longitudinis, in mucronē sensim turbinata, uelut erupturi partus inuolucrū, quæ cū dehiscens sese pandit, purpureū cornu in acumē fastigiatū demonstrat. Ea feminis incremēto distenta dissilit in rimam, & tandē elanguescēs flaccescit, subarescēs'q perit relicto cornu. cuius imā partē racemosus fructus ambit, acinis prima pubertate uirentibus, & per adolescentiā cocci rubore rutilātibus, gustu mordaci, odore uiroso, quandiu ianthinum illud exerit cornu: radice bulbosa, tenui libro uestita. nascitur in opacis sepibus. Sed & iam in hortis feritur, spectabili hiantis draconis forma, solido cornu perinde quasi lingua, cōcauo uaginæ sinu ceu rictu serpentis emicāte. Nec quis poterit inficiari, hāc esse herbā quā serpentariam nomināt officinę. Nā ueteribus Romanis & colubrinæ & serpētalis usus nominis increbuerat, nec aptius ei uocabulum potuit usurpari, cum caulis glaber, purpureis respersus lituris, uersicolori facie corpus anguinuum repræsentat & æquat longitudine, uertex quoque sinuoso oris hiatu linguam exerens cruentam caput exprimit. Dracunculus triplici effigie Plinio demonstratus est, folijs betæ, non sine thyrso, flore purpureo. hic, ut inquit, est similis aro. ...attributes by name to the first cyclamen, calling it *ichthyotheron* (fish-hunter), from the hunting of fish. A drachma of these berries, taken in two cyathi of white wine for forty days, gradually draws out the spleen through the urine and the bowels; they are drunk by the orthopneic. They purge the remains of childbirth for women.

### Dracunculus. Chapter XCVI

The greater *Dracunculus*, as Dioscorides left witnessed, grows in shaded places and around fences, with a smooth and glabrous stalk, straight, two cubits high, the thickness of a staff, with the variegated spots of dragons, distinguished by numerous purple markings, with leaves like sorrel, opposite in mutual embrace. It makes a fruit at the top of the stalk, racemose, of a color between gray at the beginning, later when it has ripened, blushing with saffron and crimson, with a large, white, round root, covered with a thin bark. It is gathered when it blackens with maturity. But this seems to me supposititious, especially since both Galen and Paul, who are accustomed to report the sayings of this author in good faith, make mention of only one *dracunculus*. The suspicion was also increased that no trace of this drawing is shown among the ancients, who everywhere adhered to the tenets of Dioscorides; and if the most ancient codices are consulted, they will finally be found to have noted no difference between the lesser and greater *dracunculus*. But which will be called the lesser, when a height of two cubits is assigned to the stalk of each? Wherefore, we suspect that the chapter which is dedicated to the greater *dracunculus* has accrued to the history of Dioscorides, especially since both claim the same appearance, size, habit, variegated skin, and native places for themselves. For both grow in shaded places around hedges and thickets, with a round root clothed in a thin bark, a straight stalk, two cubits high, the thickness of a staff, with the variegated spots of snakes, with purple markings intervening, with fruit in a raceme at the summit, the berries first green in pallor; wherefore in one it is read as gray, in the other as herbaceous. Which, when they have ripened, blush with the color of saffron or crimson. But what would trouble the reader most of all is that they seem to differ much in the leaves; in one they are designated as sorrel, in the other as ivy-like. But they exit into much more distant angles, nor are they rounded with the legitimate compass of ivy. Dioscorides explained the appearance of this leaf in his mention of *hemionium*. For he represented *hemionium* with the leaf of *dracunculus*, which is very long and almost the shape of sorrel. Hence our common people, by their custom, call *hemionium* the tongue of the deer. Wherefore, so that all suspicion may depart, we believe there is only one genus of *dracunculus*, represented by a double history, yet we judge the former to have been an addition, and to have emerged from the workshop not of Dioscorides, but of another author. Add that the virtues, even if they are described with various words, are found not to be much different or abhorrent from one another. In our region, it is found frequently enough, and is studiously cultivated in gardens, a miracle of a playful nature, and of a dragon learning to make rudiments in plants. *Dracunculus* rises with a simple stalk, two cubits high, smooth and glabrous, the thickness of a staff, variegated with the colored spots of snakes, with purple markings also intervening, so that it clearly seems to feign the habit and color of a serpent. At the leafy summit, leaves emerge, six or seven in number, hanging down like fingers on a thick petiole, sprinkled with whitish marks, of the shape of sorrel, but of a longer, ivy-like appearance. From the leafy top of the scape, a certain sheath emerges, herbaceous on the outside, almost a cubit in length, gradually tapering to a point, as if it were an involucrum for a birth about to erupt, which, when it splits and unfolds itself, shows a purple horn tapered to a point. Distended by the growth of the seeds, it splits into a fissure, and finally, weakening, it grows flaccid, and dries up and perishes, leaving the horn. The racemose fruit surrounds its lower part, with berries green in their first maturity, and reddening with the color of kermes during their youth, with a biting taste and a rank odor, as long as it puts forth that violet-colored horn; with a bulbous root, clothed in a thin bark. It grows in shaded hedges. But it is now also sown in gardens, in the spectacular form of a gaping dragon, with a solid horn appearing as if it were a tongue, and the concave hollow of the sheath like the maw of a serpent. Nor can anyone deny that this is the herb which the apothecaries call *serpentaria*. For among the ancient Romans, the use of the name *colubrina* and *serpentaria* had become common, nor could a more apt word be used for it, since the smooth stalk, sprinkled with purple marks, represents and equals the body of a snake in its variegated appearance and length, and the summit, also with the winding maw of the mouth, expresses a head protruding a bloody tongue. *Dracunculus* is shown by Pliny in triple form: with leaves of beet, not without a thyrsus, and a purple flower; this, as he says, is similar to *arum*. Others have shown it with a long root as if marked with joints, and with three stalks in total. The third demonstration...

translation:
C.P. to Nepos, Greetings.
You ask that I take care to review and amend my little books, which you have so eagerly acquired. I shall do it; for what should I more willingly undertake, especially when you request it? For since a man most grave, most learned, most eloquent, and—above all—most occupied, who is about to be a provincial governor, thinks it of such importance to carry our writings about with him, I must take care that this part of his baggage does not offend you as if it were superfluous. I will strive, therefore, first that you may have these companions as convenient as possible; and second, that when you return, you may find others that you would wish to add to them. For you, as my reader, do not encourage me to new works in a mediocre way. Farewell.

C.P. to Falco, Greetings.
It is the third day since I heard Sentius Augurinus with my greatest pleasure, or rather, admiration. He calls them poems. Many things were handled delicately, many sublimely, many with charm, many very tenderly, many sweetly, many with bite. I think that for some years, nothing of this same genre has been written more gravely or perfectly, unless perhaps his love for me deceives me, or the fact that he carried me himself to the heights with his praises. For he took for his theme the subject that I sometimes play with in verse. And so, I will make you the judge of my judgment if the second verse occurs to you from this theme; for I hold the rest, and I have already explained them:
"I sing songs in slight verses,
In the same way that my Catullus once did."

Hanc igitur chartarum memoriam, cum ad verbi vnius scientiam traduxissem ex illo didici etiam multas res, hoc modo vnius verbi continere. Inde excolendo inuentum totam vnam lectionem, & quæ in ea continerentur. Post etiam illa inueniri & ex autoribus deriuare. Vide modus ille ex temporanee profitendi. Sed reuertor ad chartarum lusum, nam hoc genus ludi est artificiosissimum, cum in certa re, & vi naturæ consisteret, omisi exercitationem illius diuinationis multis ex causis. Primum enim me statim contuli Patauium, inde in Saccense oppidum, atque ita occasio sublata illius ludi; nam ea fors non habet locum, vbi ludo industria commiscetur. Deinde quòd timerem, ne nimis fidendo me euerteret. Præterea dicebam si ex Demone est falx, est & contra legem, si fortuita stultum est illi fide. Abhorrebam etiam à ludi genere damnato legibus. Præterea stultum existimaui, cum possem locupletiore conditione, securiore scilicet, & ex naturali ratione pendente certare velle tam absurde inniti.

### CAPVT XXIV.
*De differentia ludi Chartarum à ludo Aleæ.*

DIfferunt ludi Chartarum à ludis Aleæ, in quibus industria locú habet, quòd Alea de futuro iudicium fert, & magis licet de alieno successu, tamen etiam de proprio, Chartarum autem ludi de præsentibus, & alienis solum iudicium requirunt. At de præsentibus coniectari, prudentis est magis viri, & humanæ sapientis; de futuris autem quamquam fit alia ratio coniecturæ, non quod futura fint, sed cui potius iure innitendum fit, est tamen diuini potius hominis, aut infani, ham melancholici diuinare folent. Etenim in Alea nil habes certum signum, sed omnia planè in pura fortuna reposita sunt, si alea æqualis fit. Quicquid autem est in ea præter leuem coniecturam, & rationes superius dictas ad temeritatem referri debet. At in chartis, quas posuit vultus chartarum à tergo agnitio, milleque aliæ agnitiones naturales, & dignæ, prudenti viro habentur. Vnde inter omnes ludos subtilitate præcedit, is, qui latrunculus fit. Sed fortunæ arbitrio parum, aut nihil subiacet, vtilitate armorum, salubritate pilæ: lepore: trapolæ: pulchritudine inuenti, & mopore primaria, pecuniarum magnitudine sanctius, concertatione assiduæ, quæ parum fatigat fritillus, extractione temporis tarochi: Dignitate Cricones, prudentia, & vitæ humanæ imitatione triumphi. Decet igitur sapientem chartis ludere, quàm alea, & triumphis potiùs, quàm aliis ludis, constat ergo, (sed in vsu non est) quòd medius quidam est modus ludendi chartis apertis, proximior ferte latrunculorum ludo. Et finem habet, cû nil amplius expectet; sed quilibet ludus sibi finem facit. Atque is, est qui nouem cum chartis, (nam hic est numerus fatis idoneus) ac mediocris inter magnum, & paruum ad ludendum, detectis, inde certare, vt solent cum occultis. Demiror autem hic fit ingeniosissimus, solum neglectum à tot gentibus esse.

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Decorative floral ornament</image-desc>

### CAPVT XXV.
*De ludis Chartarum.*

LDi igitur Chartarum, nó in expectatione futurorum sunt nisi cùm commutantur. Suntque earum plura genera, sed numerare non licet: Nam quòd dixit Horatius de verbis, idem de ludis dicere conuenit: fatis erit eos distinguere generibus suis, ac speciebus, tum simplicibus, tum compositis. Prima igitur genera sunt lusus arbitrio folius fortunæ, & cum industria. Fortunæ folius sunt primaria fluxus, qui fit cum tribus chartis: Gallicus est pulcherrimus, nam vnum cum figura, vel cum binario efficit xxi. qui summus est punctus apud reliquas, pleraque gentes. Sed apud Gallos, si adfit aliud vnum fiunt viginti vnum cum dimidio. Sed tria puncta superant etiam fluxum, & est supremum, & pro fluxu, & puncto haberi potest. Viginti etiam cum vno puncto, alia in charta efficit viginti cum dimidio, & ita habent viginti, viginti cum dimidio, viginti vnum, & viginti vnum cum dimidio, & viginti duo, qui (vt dixi) superior est fluxui. Post est fluxada: filerium, idest, ego habeo, quadriginta, & triginta vnum, Baseta ludus desperatorum, Cricones, fortunæ, & industria, triumphi, triumfeti, sequentie, sequentium tarochi, centum, trapola, Romfa, scaltara, tum alij mult. Alia diuisio est penè differentias proprias, quoniam ludi quidam tetinent æstimationem chartarum, alij non retinent, sed mutant. Alij numero chartarum, alij æstimatione, alij consequentibus, alij certa ratione loci, seu ordinis, aut proprietate conficiunt numerum, quòd superiores, aut inferiores euadunt:

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Decorative floral ornament</image-desc>

### CAPVT XXVI.
*An iidem doceant, & sciant.*

FOrfan meritò quis rogare posset, an iidem, qui has rationes norunt, bene ludant, an non? Videtur enim alia res scire, atque exequi, pluresque, qui optimè ludunt, esse maximè infortunati. Sed & in aliis tractationibus, eadem quæstio manet. Vtrum-ne Medicus idem sciens, & expertus? At in his, quibus tempus consilio datur, idem est sciens, atque bene fortunatus, vt in Mathematicis, Iurisprudentia, & Medicina. Rarissimè enim æger non dat moras. At in his, quibus tempus datur, & dolus præualet, aliud est scire, aliud feliciter exercere; vt in ludo, in bello, in monomachia, in mercatura. Dolus enim, et arte costet, & exercitatione, plus tamen potest exercitatio, & experientia, quàm scientia. Corporea etiam quædam cognitio plus valet in his, quibus, ea opus est scientia ipsa. Velut in gemmarum æstimatione, pictura, cognitione.

Having therefore transferred this memory of cards to the knowledge of a single word, I learned from it also many things, in this way of containing [information] within a single word. Then, by cultivating the discovery, [I learned] an entire lecture and what was contained in it. Afterwards, [I learned] to find those things and to derive them from authors. See that method of performing extemporaneously. But I return to the card game, for this kind of game is most artificial. Since it consists in a certain thing and by the force of nature, I omitted the exercise of that divination for many reasons. For first, I betook myself immediately to Padua, then to the town of Saccense, and thus the occasion for that game was removed; for that luck has no place where industry is mixed with play. Next, because I feared lest by trusting too much it might overturn me. Furthermore, I used to say if it is from a Demon, it is false, and it is also against the law; if it is fortuitous, it is foolish to trust in it. I also abhorred a kind of game condemned by the laws. Furthermore, I considered it foolish, when I could compete in a wealthier condition—namely, a more secure one, depending on natural reason—to want to rely so absurdly.

### CHAPTER XXIV.
*On the difference between the game of cards and the game of dice.*

Games of cards differ from games of dice, in which industry has a place, in that the die carries a judgment about the future, and although one may make judgments about the success of others, one also does so about one's own; however, games of cards require a judgment only about the present and the things of others. But to conjecture about present things is for a more prudent man and one wise in human affairs; but about future things, although there is another reason for conjecture—not because they are future, but as to whom it is more rightfully to be relied upon—it is nevertheless for a man more divine, or an insane one, for melancholic people are accustomed to divine. For in dice, you have no certain sign, but all things are placed entirely in pure fortune, if the die is fair. Whatever is in it beyond a slight conjecture and the reasons stated above should be referred to rashness. But in cards, the recognition of the faces of the cards from the back, and a thousand other natural and worthy recognitions, are considered by a prudent man. Hence, among all games, the one which is <term>latrunculus</term> <gloss>chess-like game/small soldiers</gloss> precedes [them] in subtlety. But there is little or nothing subject to the arbitrariness of fortune, [such as] the utility of weapons, the healthiness of the ball, the charm of <term>trapola</term>, the beauty of the invention, and the [strategy] of <term>primaria</term>, the greatness of money [being] more sacred, the constant competition which fatigues little in the dice box, the extraction of time in <term>tarochi</term>, the dignity in <term>Cricones</term>, the prudence and imitation of human life in <term>triumphi</term>. It is therefore more fitting for a wise man to play with cards than with dice, and with <term>triumphi</term> rather than other games. It is established, therefore—but it is not in use—that there is a certain intermediate method of playing with open cards, closer to the game of <term>latrunculi</term>. And it has an end, when nothing more is expected; but every game makes its own end. And it is that which uses nine cards (for this is a number sufficiently suitable and moderate between great and small for playing), [which are] revealed, then to compete, as they are accustomed to do with hidden ones. I wonder, however, why this most ingenious [game] has been neglected by so many peoples.

<note>A decorative floral ornament appears here.</note>

### CHAPTER XXV.
*On games of cards.*

Games of cards, therefore, are not in the expectation of future things, unless when they are exchanged. And there are many kinds of them, but it is not permitted to list them; for what Horace said about words, it is fitting to say the same about games: it will be sufficient to distinguish them by their genera and species, both simple and composite. The first kinds, therefore, are games of the will of fortune alone, and with industry. Those of fortune alone are <term>primaria</term> and <term>fluxus</term>, which is done with three cards: the French one is the most beautiful, for one [card] with a figure, or with a deuce, makes 21, which is the highest point among most peoples. But among the French, if another ace is present, they make twenty-one and a half. But three points exceed even the <term>fluxus</term>, and it is supreme, and can be held for both <term>fluxus</term> and point. Twenty also with one point, another [card] in the card makes twenty and a half, and thus they have twenty, twenty and a half, twenty-one, and twenty-one and a half, and twenty-two, which (as I said) is superior to the <term>fluxus</term>. After that is <term>fluxada</term>, <term>filerium</term> (that is, "I have"), forty, and thirty-one, <term>Baseta</term>, the game of desperate men, <term>Cricones</term>, [games of] fortune and industry, <term>triumphi</term>, <term>triumfeti</term>, <term>sequentie</term>, <term>sequentium tarochi</term>, <term>centum</term>, <term>trapola</term>, <term>Romfa</term>, <term>scaltara</term>, and then many others. Another division is according to its own differences, since some games retain the estimation of cards, others do not retain [them], but change [them]. Some accomplish the number by the number of cards, others by estimation, others by sequences, others by a certain reason of place, or order, or property, so that they turn out superior or inferior.

<note>A decorative floral ornament appears here.</note>

### CHAPTER XXVI.
*Whether the same people teach and know.*

Perhaps someone might rightly ask whether the same people who know these reasons play well, or not? For it seems to be one thing to know and another to execute, and many who play excellently are the most unfortunate. But in other treatises, the same question remains. Is the doctor both knowledgeable and experienced? But in these matters, in which time is given for counsel, the same person is knowledgeable and well-fortunate, as in mathematics, jurisprudence, and medicine. For very rarely does a patient not allow for delays. But in these matters, in which time is given and trickery prevails, it is one thing to know and another to exercise happily, as in games, in war, in single combat, in commerce. For trickery consists of both art and exercise, yet exercise and experience can do more than science. Also, certain bodily cognition is worth more in those things in which it is needed than the science itself. As in the estimation of gems, painting, and cognition.

translation: Half-gods, they were able to conquer through immense circles of the world. The insane love of Mars and the ardor of unholy war consumed these near the seven gates of Cadmus for the sake of Oedipus’s empire. And the waves of the resounding sea consumed these, when the Argolic fleets sought Pergamum <note>Troy</note>, where the pale image of death leaned from above, while the daughter of Tyndarus <note>Helen</note> was avenged by a just sword. Jupiter also divided these from the whole world and granted them a better use of life, and gave them the hills of the deep to inhabit, at the shore of the ocean. A happy and holy progeny! Here, where the earth is verdant, where the most fertile nurse, the earth, pours forth sweet fruits three times a year from her lap. If the Fates had not created me with the fifth race, but allowed me to die before or to be born after, I would have preferred it. Now, it is an iron age, which cares and a thousand labors press upon by night and day, and gradually press toward its destruction. Thus it pleased the gods, but prosperous fates will also arrive sometime in the whirlwind of things. Nor will this unspeakable age of men be destroyed any less, when their times are ripe with years and their hair turns gray. Children will not be like their parents as before, nor parents like their children, nor will a guest be safe with a host. Friends will corrupt the holy bond, and discord will rage, stirring up arms among brothers. The hurried old age of men will live devoid of honor, and there will be no shame in chiding parents broken by old age. An unhappy offspring, it knows not the law and the precepts of the gods, and does not provide these foods for an invalid parent.

When our adversaries noticed that this orthodox view conflicted with their own hypothesis about the three parts of man, they substituted a false foundation for regeneration. They profess that a person is regenerated not through the heard or read Word, which is endowed with divine power, but immediately through an internal light. They imagine that a small spark of this light remains in the hearts of all people after the Fall. They claim that by the internal secret powers and touches of this light alone, a person is converted from evil to good. They believe this happens so completely that they do not even require knowledge of the external history of the death and satisfaction of Christ to achieve its salvific effect.

For this reason, <term>Barclay</term> <gloss>Robert Barclay, a prominent Quaker theologian</gloss> establishes in his *Theses on the True Christian Divinity* <note>original: "Relig. vere Christi Thes."</note>, thesis 4, sections 14 and 16, that this spirit naturally leavens a person so that many can feel the power of this divine and holy seed. Through it, they are converted from evil to good, even if they are entirely ignorant of Christ's arrival on earth, through whose benefit of obedience and passion we enjoy this grace. Therefore, we are not surprised by those who teach that the unity of the faithful is found not in unity of confession, but in the unity of the Spirit. They say all should be called true Christians and brothers as long as they are united by the spirit and walk according to the spirit, even if they differ not only in rituals but also in their confession of the mysteries of faith. However, they believe that those who bear the fruit of the flesh or the external man should be regarded as heathens, whether they are clergy or laypeople, even if they agree in their confession of the mysteries. It is publicly known that this mockery was recently cast about in Halberstadt by this group, which prides itself on the title of <term>Pietism</term> <gloss>a movement emphasizing individual piety over formal doctrine</gloss>. This alone shows which spirit dictated these things to his sons and daughters there. 

Furthermore, they make the entire work of regeneration depend on the internal listening to the Spirit speaking immediately, without the cooperation of the external Word, whether read or heard. Hence, <term>Schwenckfeld</term> <gloss>Caspar von Schwenckfeld, a 16th-century mystic</gloss> teaches in his book *On the Word* that people can be converted and saved without external preaching. He claims there is no path for the Word to travel; this is an inept <term>metabasis eis allo genos</term> <gloss>a shift into a different category of being</gloss>. He argues there is no passage from the eyes and ears to the heart; therefore, Scripture and the sacraments cannot reach the heart but remain only with the external senses and the external man.

## XXIV.

Since the divine virtue of perfected Eloquence enjoys the same breadth as human knowledge, is bounded by clearly the same limits, and extends its reach to everything that can be grasped by the intellect, (a) not a few who were destined to fulfill the name of a perfect Orator have applied themselves with diligent care to this: that they might acquire for themselves the faculty of speaking, even on the spot, about any theme proposed to them. I do not wish to survey the most ancient times and bring forth from them *Gorgias of Leontini*, the disciple of *Empedocles*, *who so surpassed all others of his age in literary studies that he was the first to make a habit of asking in an assembly what subject anyone wished to hear about*; (b) for to one turning his eyes toward more recent centuries, there appear a great number who have both displayed an extemporaneous faculty of speaking on any subject and have shared the method for aspiring to it with the learned world through writings sent out into public light. Among these, *Raymundus Lullus* <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher, logician, and Franciscan friar from Majorca known for his "Art"—a system of symbolic logic intended to find the truth in any field of knowledge.</note> sustained the attempt of something unique; he was a Master of the Liberal Arts and a Professor of Sacred Theology, born in the City of the Greater Balearic Islands, *called Palma by the ancients*, and descended from the noble lineage of the *Lulls of Barcelona*. (c) For he, besides other monuments of his genius—

a) *This is evident from the definition of Rhetoric handed down by Aristotle in Rhetoric, book 1, chapter 2:* <note>original Greek: "ἔστω δ' ἡ ῥητορικὴ δύναμις περὶ ἕκαστον τοῦ θεωρῆσαι τὸ ἐνδεχόμενον πιθανόν"</note> Let Rhetoric be the faculty OF DISCERNING IN EACH CASE what is capable of persuading. *This is also sufficiently clear from the words immediately following this definition, which in the version by George of Trebizond* <note>A 15th-century Greek philosopher and scholar who was a key figure in the revival of Greek letters in the West.</note> *read as follows: This is the duty of no other art. For individual arts are instructional and persuasive concerning that which is subject to them, such as medicine concerning what can be healed or be sick, Geometry concerning the properties that happen to magnitudes, Arithmetic concerning number, and similarly the remaining arts and sciences. But Rhetoric seems to be able to see clearly the credible elements concerning any given matter, so to speak. Therefore, we also say that THIS ART IS NOT CONCERNED WITH ANY SPECIFIC DETERMINED GENRE.*
b) *These are the words of Valerius Maximus, book 8, chapter 15. Add also Cicero, On the Orator, book 1, section 22; book 3, section 32; and On Ends, book 2, at the beginning; and Quintilian, Institutes of Oratory, book 12, chapter 11, page 914.*

# CAPUT IV.

### Territorium, oppida, & castella Eugubinorum.

I. Territorii Eugubini qui fines fuerint antiquiori tempore, cum Romani rerum potiebantur, ac multo magis ante Romanos, frustra aliquis quaereret. Id unum liquet ad Eugubinos pertinuisse quidquid inter has civitates iacebat, quarum non una erat distantia, Sentinum, Tadinum, Nuceriam, Assisium, Perusium, Tifernum, & Callium. Post autem, cum barbari Italiae statum turbassent, Tadino destructo, aliisque civitatibus afflictis, id emolumenti ex communi clade Eugubini consecuti sunt, ut ultra antiquos fines eorum pertica percurrerit. Itaque pars agri Tadinatis ipsis attributa videtur, quod & de Sentinati, & Calliensi, & aliarum fortasse civitatum accidisse censeo. Nullibi vero magis prolati sunt fines agri Eugubini, quam ex ea parte, quae est inter Callium, & Sentinum, ultra Pergulam ab ipsis conditum, & Montem Siccum, alias Montem Siconis, quae loca ultra fines Calliensium, & Sentinatium iacebant, & forte ad Suafanos pertinebant, antiquam civitatem ad ripam amnis cognominis positam(a), quo nunc amne oppidum Per-

from the patricians and partly from the commoners, according to ancient custom and the prescription of their own laws. The one who holds the first place of dignity among them is called the <term>vexillifer iustitiae</term> <gloss>standard-bearer of justice</gloss>. He is from the order of patricians, to whom is added a colleague from the same order, called the colleague of the standard-bearer. The remaining six are from the lower order, namely from the practitioners of the arts, and they retain that ancient name of consuls. And these eight hold the magistracy for a period of two months. Their power is not insignificant, nor are the insignia and ornaments of their dignity few or common; and they are much greater in the extraordinary magistracy, which is created each year from the primary patricians on the feast of S. Ubaldus, to whom the other magistrates lower their rods and grant supreme power in the city. They call him the Constable. But it is not for this place to narrate these matters further.

# CHAPTER IV.

### The territory, towns, and castles of the Eugubini.

I. One would seek in vain what the boundaries of the Eugubine territory were in earlier times, when the Romans held power, and even more so before the Romans. This alone is clear: that whatever lay between these cities, the distance between which was not uniform—Sentinum, Tadinum, Nuceria, Assisium, Perusium, Tifernum, and Callium—pertained to the Eugubini. However, later, when the barbarians had disturbed the state of Italy, with Tadinum destroyed and other cities afflicted, the Eugubini gained this benefit from the common disaster: their reach extended beyond the ancient borders. Thus, a part of the Tadinum region seems to have been attributed to them, which I believe also happened with the Sentinum and Callium regions, and perhaps those of other cities. In no place, however, were the boundaries of the Eugubine territory extended more than on the side that lies between Callium and Sentinum, beyond Pergula, founded by them, and Mons Siccus, otherwise <term>Mons Siconis</term> <gloss>Mount Siconis</gloss>, which places lay beyond the borders of the Callium and Sentinum peoples and perhaps belonged to the Suafani, an ancient city situated on the bank of the river of the same name <margin>(a)</margin>, by which river the town of Per-

<header>Sixth Book</header>

into two parts. Why, however, was the tremor for many days? For Campania did not cease to tremble continuously, more gently indeed, but with immense damage, as it shook what was pressed and shattered. For those things which were distressing it for falling, it was not to be pushed, but to be agitated. Clearly, not all the spirit had exited yet, but with the greater part of itself emitted, it still wandered. Among the arguments by which it is proven that these things are done by spirit, there is no reason why you should doubt to place this also: when the greatest tremor is issued, by which cities and lands have been ravaged, nor can another follow it afterwards, but after the greatest force, the tremors are light, which it made more vehemently when the winds were struggling for an exit. Then the remains of the residual spirit cannot do the same, nor is there need for a fight for them, since they have already found a way, and they follow that by which the first and greatest force escaped. I also judge this worthy of memory to be known by a most learned and serious man: for by chance, when it happened, he was bathing. He affirmed that he saw in the bath the Thessalian tiles, with which the floor was paved, being separated one from the other, and thus being joined and separated; and the water was sometimes received into the fissures as the pavement receded, sometimes boiled and was expelled when it was compressed. I heard the same man telling that he saw soft materials tremble more softly and more frequently than the hard nature. Nor is it, O Lucilius, a man excellent regarding the causes themselves. These things now which pertain to the strengthening of minds, which it is more important to become stronger by nature than more learned. If one is not made without the other. For strength does not come to the mind from elsewhere than from good arts, than from the contemplation of nature. For what has this very calamity not strengthened and raised up against everyone? For why should I fear a man or even a beast? Why should I fear a dart or a spear?

<meta>This page continues Robert Hooke's technical description of the mechanical components used in his high-precision astronomical instruments. He focuses here on the "Centres and Sockets" that allow for the fine adjustment and measurement of angles.</meta>

The way the **centers** and **sockets** are designed can be seen in Figures 12 and 13. Figure 13 shows them in an end-view **perspective**, while Figure 12 shows a side-view **perspective**. Number 1 is the roller <note>original: "Rowler"; a cylindrical component used to rotate or move parts of the instrument</note> of the upper tube, and 2 is the roller of the lower tube. 3 3 are the screws used to fasten them in the holes. 4 4 is the enclosing or socket-screw that presses tightly against the **cylinder**. 5 and 6 indicate the smooth cylindrical socket that guides the cylindrical screw, ensuring its axis passes exactly over the center of the roller 2 2. By using a **ring (7)** on the screw, the pointed end (8) is held against the support <note>original: "portance"; a bearing or supporting part</note> (9). It is not difficult to understand how to make a dividing plate and its hand or pointer <note>original: "Index"; a pointer on a scientific instrument</note>, nor how it can be turned from the center of the two tubes by a long rod, as shown in *Figure 8*. Once it is determined through observation how many rotations (and what fraction of a rotation) correspond to five whole degrees, it will be easy to calculate a table of *subtenses* <note>original: "Subtenses"; linear measurements used to determine the size of an angle; effectively a table of chords</note>. This table will show exactly what fraction of a turn is needed to measure every minute and second of that angle.

3. In 1665, I achieved the same result using a roller that rolled along the edge <note>original: "limb"; the graduated arc or outer edge of an astronomical instrument</note> of the **quadrant**. This was done with the help of two wires coiled around those rollers, with their ends fastened to the edge of the **quadrant**. By using a large pointer on the end of this roller, I was able to move the arm of the instrument to any five-second interval on the **quadrant** with great ease and certainty.

At the same time, I also built another frame with a straight screw that opened only to five degrees. This used rollers <note>original: "Tumbrels"; here used to describe small cylinders or wheels within the mechanism</note> similar to a pair of dividing *compasses* (using the same method I just described for measuring *diameters* or *distances* up to five degrees). I used very precise <note>original: "curious"; in this period, the word meant highly detailed, expert, or intricately made</note> lines drawn on a smooth glass plate and points very precisely marked at every five degrees on the edge of the **quadrant** (or whatever instrument it was attached to). With the help of a very thick *plano-convex lens* (with its flat side facing down toward the plate and the curved side toward the eye), this frame could be moved five degrees at a time across the entire edge of the **quadrant**. Using this instrument, I could easily and accurately divide an angle into five-second increments.

# IN VERREM LIB. IIII.

The severity of the crime does not allow me to keep silent. Judges, there is an ancient belief, established by the oldest Greek writings and monuments, that the entire island of Sicily is consecrated to Ceres and Libera <note>Greek: Demeter and Persephone.</note>. Not only do other nations believe this, but the Sicilians themselves are so persuaded of it that it seems ingrained and innate in their minds. They believe that these goddesses were born in these very places, that the crops were first discovered in this land, and that Libera—whom they also call Proserpina—was abducted from the grove of Enna, a place located in the center of the island, which is called the navel of Sicily. It is said that when Ceres wished to search for her, she lit torches from the fires that erupt from the peak of Mount Aetna. Carrying these, she traveled over the entire globe. 

Enna, where these events are said to have occurred, is on a high and elevated spot. At its summit is a flat plain with perennial water, yet the whole place is cut off and surrounded by steep approaches. Around it are many lakes, groves, and the finest flowers at every time of year, as if the place itself were meant to illustrate the abduction of the maiden that we have heard of since we were boys. Nearby is a cave facing north, of infinite depth, where they say Father Dis <note>The god of the underworld, Pluto.</note> suddenly emerged with his chariot and carried the maiden away, descending suddenly under the earth not far from Syracuse. A lake appeared in that very spot, where, to this day, the Syracusans hold annual festivals with a great gathering of men and women. Because of the antiquity of this belief, and because traces—almost the cradle—of their history are found in these places...

> Which thinks in men is the nature of their limbs,
> In each and every person; for the dominant element is thought."<sup>3</sup>

He thus considers sensation and thought to be the same thing. He believes that memory and forgetfulness arise from the mixing of these elements, but he leaves it quite unclear whether they hold equal weight in the mixture, whether this constitutes thought or not, and what exactly this condition is. "...with great force, he invaded all of India, as there was no city of significant size able to withstand him. However, because of the intense heat, his soldiers began to die from a plague-like disease, until that wise general led his troops from the plains up into the mountains. There, the gusts of cool winds and the pure waters flowing from the mountain springs cured the army of the plague. The place where Bacchus refreshed his forces was called (1) *Meros*. After this, dedicating himself to the cultivation <note>original: "husbanding"</note> of fruit, he shared his knowledge with the Indians and taught them the invention of wine and other things useful for life. Besides this, he was the founder of many great cities, moving the inhabitants of small villages to more conveniently situated locations. After he had reigned over all of India for fifty-two years, he died of old age. His sons then took over the government, passing it down to their own sons. "Suppose Christmas now approaching, the ever-green ivy trimming and adorning the portals and partitions of so frequented a building; the usual carols, to observe antiquity, cheerfully sounding; and that which is the complement of his inferior comforts, his neighbors, whom he tenders as members of his own family, join with him in this consort of mirth and melody." p. 80. In the second Part, p. 27, he calls a piper "an ill wind that begins to blow upon Christmas Eve, and so continues, very loud and blustering, all the twelve days: or an airy meteor, composed of flatuous matter, that then appears, and vanishes, to the great peace of the whole family, the thirteenth day."
