Et notandum cum his / quod sperma vulgatum fixum est / et tum corpore mortuo suo in sensitivam virtutem abit et sumit corpus sensitivum (alias insensitivum) ex corpore insensitivo sicut in elementis / quia muscarum generatio ex aëre procedit / lacertarum ex terra / araneae ex igne / serpentes vero ex aqua (pulices e mineralibus. Die fliegen und Lacerten seind alle Käfer die nit ex stercoribus generiert werden / die fliegen wachsen ex elemento aeris / dann in elementis ist auch sperma menstruosum / aranea ex elemento ignis / id est / principium araneorum est ex elemento ignis / ex elemento aquam werden dann privative die schlangen.

## De cura Vermium.

Nunc de his quae ad curam pertinent / et sunt haec medicamina intrinseca / et quae sunt extrinseca : debet esse ex una natura. Porro oportet etiam intelligere genera intrinseca / externa medicamina. mineral substances and mineral sperms come to the stomach, it goes to the worms.

## The Fifth Paragraph.

And it is to be noted with these that common sperm is fixed, and then, with its own dead body, it departs into a sensitive virtue and assumes a sensitive body (otherwise insensitive) from an insensitive body, as in the elements; because the generation of flies proceeds from air, of lizards from earth, of spiders from fire, snakes truly from water (fleas from minerals). The flies and lizards are all beetles that are not generated from dung; the flies grow from the element of air, for in the elements there is also menstrual sperm; the spider from the element of fire, that is, the principle of spiders is from the element of fire; from the element of water then, privatively, become the snakes.

## On the Cure of Worms.

Now about those things that pertain to the cure, and these are internal medicines, and what are external: it must be from one nature. Furthermore, it is necessary to also understand the internal genera, external medicines. It is also necessary to know most perfectly the process of poison. Finally, know that every medicine that kills worms is from poison. And those that cure external worms, the same also [cure] internal ones.

whom the king has granted life) may still come closer. The imitation of linguistic usage in later philosophy, which Cumont (op. cit.) seems to emphasize, is irrelevant for the language of the mysteries; or rather, it originates from the practice of the mysteries themselves.

Thus, it might initially appear as if an old **technical term** <note>German: *terminus technicus*</note> of the Mithras religion was transferred into the Corinthian Isis mysteries. I do not wish to deny that it played a part; however, I believe I can demonstrate from a magic text, interesting in many respects, that it does not act alone. In the great Paris Magical Papyrus, we find in Wessely, *Greek Magical Papyri* (Memoirs of the Imperial-Royal Academy, 1888) p. 48, line 154 ff., the alleged writing of a priest named Nephotes to the last king of free Egypt, the "wise" Psammetichus, who—much like his counterpart Nectanebo in the *Alexander Romance*—practices **lecanomancy** <note>The art of divination using a bowl of water; from the Greek *lekane* (basin/dish).</note>. I will examine the instructions for this in a bit more detail, as they corroborate individual features of Apuleius’s description. The magician, who is accompanied by a **guide** <note>Greek: *mystagogos*; one who leads an initiate into the mysteries.</note>, is to lie down in burial clothes with his eyes bound, and moreover, closing them tightly.

So he speaks the prayer, which possesses the divine **energy** <note>original Greek: ἐνέργεια (*energeia*); here meaning effective spiritual power or activity.</note> (line 160), addressed to Seth or Typhon <note>In the Hellenistic period, the Egyptian god Seth was often identified with the Greek monster Typhon.</note> (line 179 ff.):

> Powerful Typhon, scepter-bearer and ruler of the scepter on high, god of gods, lord, I am he who together with you searched through the whole world and found the great Osiris, whom I brought to you bound; I am he who fought on your side as an ally against the gods — or (other copies): towards the gods — I am he who shut the double folds of heaven and lulled to sleep the dragon that no eye can see, who stopped the currents of the sea and the streams of rivers, until you gained mastery over this scepter-power; **I, your soldier** <note>original Greek: ὁ σὸς στρατιώτης (*ho sos stratiotes*); this is the crucial term Reitzenstein is tracking.</note>, have been conquered by the gods, I have been cast down prostrate because of a hollow wrath; arise, I entreat you, your friend, I beseech you, and do not cast me down to the earth, lord of gods; strengthen me, I entreat you, and grant me this favor, so that whenever I tell one of these gods to come through my chants, he may swiftly appear to me, having come.

# On the Revolution of the
## Late Winter, and what occurs
## therein.

<note>A decorative initial letter W.</note>
We wish to have the entire year divided into five
parts, namely:
Late Winter, Spring <note>original: "Lenz"</note>, Summer,
Autumn, and Early Winter. We shall briefly
treat three things concerning these: the arrangement <term>Disposition</term> <gloss>astrological positioning</gloss> of the heavens and their influence <term>Influentz</term> <gloss>the flowing power of the stars</gloss>, the eclipses and their significance, and then
the changes in the air <note>weather patterns</note>.

Firstly, concerning the Late Winter,
which follows immediately after the old year,
and extends from Saint Lucia's Day 1595 until Saint Gregory's Day 1596. It begins
in the preceding civil year of 1595, on the 12th day
of December <note>original: "Christmonats"</note>, in the afternoon at 4 o'clock and 40
minutes. At that time, a few days prior, the Sun <term>Sol</term> <gloss>the Sun</gloss> and Venus
set with the star Arcturus, which caused wind. Around that time, in the geographic height of the land of Basel, the 10th degree of Cancer <term>Cancri</term> <gloss>the Crab</gloss> shows itself in the morning corner. At the peak of the heavens is found the 7th degree of Pisces <note>original: "Fisch"</note>, in which
25th degree Jupiter then had its course,
and makes itself heard as a ruler on account of an exceeding prerogative <note>original: "propter nimiam prærogativam"</note>.

<summary>Thurneysser introduces his five-season division of the year and begins his analysis of the Late Winter season, starting in December 1595, with specific planetary positions for the region of Basel.</summary>

*Smelter.* But what then are the means by which I may open up <note>original: *auffschliessen*; in metallurgy, this means to break down the ore's structure to make the metal accessible</note> such ores of mine and, as you have said, free them from the earthiness they carry with them? *Mercury.* The additives for roasting are indeed diverse, as you can certainly imagine for yourself, according to the many properties of the ores. These materials are also available in almost all places; often one only needs to apply a little effort to prepare them, so that one is a match for the volatile ores, to tame and compel them; only they must be transformed and, following the nature of the earth, purified and separated from their acidic, earthy essence, and turned toward the metals. This you must learn and understand very well; then you can use all salts <note>original: *Salien*; a general term for various mineral salts</note>, whatever their names may be, as well as other ingredients such as quicklime, antimony, coal, furnace soot, sulfur pyrites, and even sand, clay, and street-sludge <note>original: *Gassen-Koth*; literally "street filth," often used in historical recipes for the minerals and nitrates found in city waste</note> (according to their preparation) quite usefully for such fixing of the ores during roasting. That is to say, the highest degree of sympathetic vibration is only to be attained through introduced tones of very narrowly limited pitch. This is the case with tuning forks and bells. The air mass of the oral cavity, on the contrary, has low density and mass; its walls, as far as they are formed by soft tissues, are not very resistant and are imperfectly elastic, having much internal friction during vibrations, through which they destroy movement. Furthermore, the vibrated air mass of the oral cavity communicates through the mouth opening with the external air and quickly gives up large parts of its received movement to it. For this very reason, a once-excited vibrating movement in the air of the oral cavity dies out very quickly, as one can easily observe if one snaps a finger against the cheek with various vowel positions of the mouth. One then distinguishes the pitch of the resonance quite well for the various transition stages of <term>O</term> on one hand toward <term>U</term> and on the other toward <term>A</term>. But the tone is very shortly decaying. Also by clicking against the teeth, one can make the different resonance of the oral cavity audible. For this very reason, a tone that oscillates nearly in agreement only for the few vibrations of such a short resonance tone can find amplification through sympathetic vibration, which turns out to be not much less than for a precisely agreeing tone; and the breadth in the scale, the tones of which can be noticeably amplified by a given position of the mouth, is quite considerable <note>See for this also Appendix X and the corresponding explanations in the text of Div. I, Section 6.</note>. This is confirmed by the experiment. If I place a resonator for <term>b'</term> to the right ear and one for <term>f''</term> to the left ear, and sing the vowel <term>O</term> on <term>B</term>, then not only is the fourth partial <term>b'</term>, which corresponds to the natural tone of the oral cavity, amplified, but quite noticeably, even if significantly less than the aforementioned, the sixth <term>f''</term> is as well. ...[of the] white and the red flowers, it is impossible, even if one already wished to prepare a composition and proceed further with it. And precisely from this spring the impure metals, when Nature does not maintain the weight, or maintains an unequal weight. Therefore, when one wishes to make a composition, the weight must be exactly struck with the ingredients <note>original Latin: *Ingredientibus*</note>, and not missed by a hair’s breadth. **Rasis** <note>Referring to Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a famous Persian alchemist and physician.</note> says: "Whoever is ignorant of weights should not labor in our books, because the philosophers have hidden nothing of their matters except this." <note>original Latin: *Quicunque ignorat pondera, non laboret in libris nostris, quia philosophi nil suarum rerum occultavereunt, nisi hoc.*</note> But when the weight is present, then they merge with one another like lard <note>implies a smooth, complete melting or blending</note>, and the mixture of the **male & female**, of the **Sulfur & Mercury** <note>original Latin: *masculi & fœminæ, Sulphuris & Mercurii*</note>, of the white and the red flowers occurs—along with other attending and belonging things—**down to the smallest parts** <note>original Latin: *per minima*</note> and **at the root** <note>original Latin: *in radice*</note>, and it is then perpetuated.

But to strike the weight and to manage its justification, the craftsman <note>original Latin: *Artifex*</note> and Nature must help one another; then the two masters of the scale find each other. The craftsman indeed uses a common scale with two bowls, such as is the custom in workshops <note>original Latin: *Officinis*</note> or pharmacies, or even with the grocer <note>original German: *Grempen* refers to a petty trader or huckster</note>, when they weigh out cheese and butter.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Elizabeth Barton’s rise to fame. The previous page ended with the description of how the corrupt commissioners, tasked with investigating her, instead fueled her delusions and declared her a chosen instrument of God.</meta>

<page-num>307</page-num>
<header>a prophetess.</header>

...had made a religious procession to her image at Court at Strete. <note>Court at Strete (now Court-at-Street) was a small hamlet in Kent where Elizabeth Barton claimed to have her first visions.</note> The commissioners, who had instigated the entire affair, organized this procession shortly thereafter, in which over 3,000 people from all walks of life gathered, and which the commissioners led with this "blessed instrument of heaven." When the procession entered the chapel, they were greeted by the *Hail, Queen of Heaven*; <note>original: "Ave Regina coelorum," a traditional Marian antiphon.</note> the Saint fell down before the image of the Holy Virgin and went into an ecstasy, during which she recited songs and speeches of praise for the Virgin Mary and the Catholic religion. She asserted that she had received a divine command to become a nun, and that the Holy Virgin wished for Doctor Bocking to be her spiritual father. It was now pretended that she had recovered from her previous illness in a miraculous manner; and after the commissioners had delivered a faithful report of everything that had occurred to the Archbishop of Canterbury, he ordained that she should be veiled as a nun in the Convent of the Holy Sepulchre <note>A Benedictine nunnery in Canterbury.</note> at Canterbury, in accordance with the will of God.

The goal of her mission appeared, at first glance, to have been reached. The chapel at Court at Strete was diligently visited and showered with gifts; the priests grew fat, and even the brother hermit <note>Likely referring to a local caretaker or anchorite at the Court at Strete chapel.</note> was no longer forced to eat water-soups. However, the nuns in the Convent of the Holy Sepulchre presumably also wanted their share of the harvest...

<summary>Elizabeth Barton is officially recognized as a miracle worker after a staged procession and "ecstatic" performance at Court at Strete. She is subsequently installed as a nun in Canterbury, bringing significant financial profit to her handlers.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>het aber das die Element an? solten das alles Element sein/so were nichts zergenglichs auff Erden. Das ist wol war/das der Leib vier Elementen an jhm hat/Werme vnnd Kälte/jha in den gesunden dingen: Was aber in der Gesundheit brochen ist/da ist kein Element mehr/da weicht Hitz vnnd Kälte hinweg/was weiter des Elements also entsetzt wird/das ist des tods eigen. Die Werme im Leib vnd Kälte/so der Mensch bedarff zu seinem Leben/das ist <term>Elementum Ignis</term>. Aber von kranckheiten zu reden/muß desselbigen alle geschwigen werden. Das Fleisch so von <term>Corrosiven</term> angegriffen wird/das ist noch bey Leben/so es aber abgeschieden wird/vnd hindann falt/darnach so ist es das/so jhr meinen/das es noch stand. So nun sein statt mit anderem Fleisch erfüllet wird/wie es der Conditor beschaffen hat/so ist dasselbige kein Fleisch mehr auß Vrsachen/es hat der Elementischen Werme nit mehr. Dann was ausserthalb dem natürlichen Samen gezogen oder gemacht wird/da hat kein Element sein wohnung in. Die Werme aber so es hat/die entlehnet es vom gesunden Fleisch auß seiner nachbarschafft. Ist gleich einem Krisensack/der hinder dem Ofen warm wird/ist ein entlehnte Werme vom Feuer das im Ofen ist: Also auch mit diesen todten dingen/haben nur gleichnuß davon/darinn sie sich auffenthalten. Aber weiter von der Werme der kranckheit zu reden/oder jhrer kälte/von wannen sie seyen oder kommen/ist etlichs theils auß der Exercitation entlehnet/wie einer der da schwitzt auß Arbeit. Dergleichen <term>Oppilationen</term> verhalten ein Ausgang/vnd fallend hauffen an/wie ein geschwell Wasser/es seind alles frembd Hitzen/da weder Complexen noch Elementen in zu schaffen haben. Vnd mercks auch hieben/so solche Hitz oder Kälte solten auß der Complex kommen/so were dir müglich/die Complexiones zu mutieren/wie es dir gefiel: dann köntestu ein Hitz brechen/so köntestu Kelte machen/& per contrarium. Aber es ist gleich als in <term>Putrefactionibus</term>, das ist/von einem Misthauffen/der auff einander ligt/vnd kalt gelegt wird/der hat ein Art an jhm/das er heisser wird/dann er dem Roß auß dem Bauch kommen ist/vnd wann er noch so heiß wird/noch ists kein Element nit/noch kein Complex des Mists nit/es ist digestum.

<margin>B</margin>Solchs alles ist allein ein Anfang der Erkanntnus zu mehrerm verstand vnd grund in die Theorie der Irrung vnd des Proces der Offnen Schäden.

Hiebey mercken auch/das in der Natur solcher Exempel vil seind/die da möchten eim einfeltigen Artzt gradus geben. Als in <term>Salibus</term>, die haben ein gleich Element/aber sie wircken auß dem Element nichts/wir mögen auch kein Element brauchen noch administrieren/dann sie sind klar in <term>Virtutibus</term>, sie lebend allein darauß/vnd wirckend nit darauß. Was aber weiter vnderscheidet sind/Als <term>Salmiar</term> gegen <term>Sal maris</term>, <term>Alumen rochum</term> gegen <term>Plumolum</term>, das ist nit der Elementen schuld/es ist der Krafft schuld/die sawr vnd süß ist/räß vnd gesalzen/aber eins hat des Elements gleich so vil/als das ander. Darumb <term>Salcedo</term>, <term>Amaritudo</term>, <term>dulcedo</term>, <term>Ponticum</term>, <term>Acerbum</term>, <term>Acetosum</term>, &c. der Art soll zu gelegt werden/vnd nit andern dingen/auch kein Complex dester höher schätzen oder weniger. Solche art ist gleich wie ein Mensch von dem andern gescheiden ist/mit der Hüpsche oder Stercke/welches des Elements art nit ist/also ist auch der <term>Salia</term> Wesen ein Art. Also ist <term>Sal Gemmæ</term> scherppfer dann <term>Sal Anathron</term>, dann je ein Mensch scherppfer dann das ander auch ist/vnd alles ausserhalb der Complex: Wie ein Zungscherpfer schneidt dann die ander/vnd sind doch alle Fleischig vnd ein Form. Vnd wie <term>Sal Gemmæ</term> hüpscher ist dann <term>Sal Anathron</term>, so muß es auch diaphinischer vnd rässer sein: Dann die Schöne gibt die <term>Exaltation</term> der Art vnd Tugend/dem leib/vnd nicht des Elements. Vnd wie der <term>Salmiar</term> stercker ist/dann <term>Sal maris</term>, das ist der Stercke schuld/wie ein Man stercker dann der ander. Nun schawend jhr von wannen die Stercke kom: dann wie es in eim mehr ist/dann im andern/also auch die scherppfe/vnd räß in eim mehr dann im andern. Die Kälte im <term>Gampffer</term> ist nicht des Elements/sie ist der Art/vnd hat ein Steublins nicht mehr/dann ein warms Wasser: Gleich als die <term>Cantharides</term> die brennend Blatern/nicht auß krafft des Element Fewers! Dann sie hand keins Steublins mehr dann die <term>Camillen</term>. <term>Nestlen</term> brennt auch/nicht von des Element Fewers wegen/sonder auß der Subtile seiner Form/deren die Art ist.

<margin>C</margin>Das sind <term>Mysteria</term> vnnd <term>Magnalia</term>/also von Gott geordnet vber die Elementen vnnd Complexiones: Vnnd was also brennt/beißt/etzt/rc. hangt der Complex eben an/als ein Wort das Maul geht: Dann als wenig das selbig Elementisch ist/also wenig sind auch die Art vnd <term>virtutes naturalium</term> der Elementen. Vnd so jhr Philosophiam mit rechtem grund vnderwinden werden/so werden ewer kranckheiten eins freyen Vrsprungs sein/vnd nit wie ein Weberzettel. Wiewol jhr solchen grundt durch euch nit erdacht haben/es langt an euch auß der Philosophen/die doch zu der Medicin in kein weg gebraucht soll werden/mit solchem jrsal vnd vbel gegründter Doctorey. Dann es wird <term>Aristoteles</term> <term>Auerrois</term> <term>Albertus</term>, vnnd ander/in solchen <term>Naturalibus</term>, kein sitz haben/dann jnen ist der Artzney nichts befohlen gesein/daß sie also mit solchem gewalt sollen erhalten werden/vnnd jhr wissend/das jhr Philosophen Lehr/vnd dergleichen/ohn alle Experienz in die Bücher gesetzt ist/welches doch in kein weg in der Artzney statt oder Platz haben soll.

->Darumb ich billich sag/das auß eim Artzt der Philosophus geboren soll werden/vnd nit das Widerspil. Solchs zu probieren/vnd euch an tag zu legen/beweisend ewer eigen Händ/Künst vnd Facultas.<-

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s argument that diseases—specifically "open sores" or ulcers—are not caused by an imbalance of the four primary elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) or the traditional "complexions" (temperaments). He argues that the heat of a fever or the "burning" of a salt is a specific property of that substance's nature, not the literal Element of Fire.</meta>

<page-num>379</page-num>
# On Open Sores / The First Book

<margin>A</margin>Does this, however, concern the elements? If everything were made only of elements, then nothing on Earth would be perishable. It is indeed true that the body has the four elements within it—warmth and cold—at least in healthy things. But when health is broken, the element is no longer there; heat and cold depart. Whatever is thus displaced from the element belongs to death. The warmth and cold in the body that a human requires for life is the <term>Element of Fire</term> <note>original: "Elementum Ignis"</note>. But when speaking of diseases, all of that must be set aside. Flesh that is attacked by <term>corrosives</term> <note>substances that eat away at body tissue</note> is still part of the living; but once it is separated and falls away, it becomes that which you [traditional doctors] mistakenly believe still stands as part of the body. Now, if its place is filled with other flesh, as the Creator ordained, that new growth is no longer "flesh" in the same sense, because it no longer possesses that elemental warmth. For whatever is pulled or made outside of the natural seed has no element dwelling within it. The warmth it does have is borrowed from the healthy flesh in its neighborhood. It is just like a <term>grain sack</term> <note>original: "Krisensack," a bag filled with grain or herbs used as a heat compress</note> that becomes warm behind the stove; it is a borrowed warmth from the fire inside the stove. So it is with these dead things; they only have a resemblance to life in which they maintain themselves. 

But to speak further of the heat of disease, or its cold—from whence they come—it is partly borrowed from <term>exertion</term> <note>original: "Exercitation"</note>, like one who sweats from labor. Similarly, <term>obstructions</term> <note>original: "Oppilationen," blockages of the body's vessels or pores</note> prevent an exit and cause a buildup, like dammed-up water. These are all "foreign" heats, in which neither the <term>complexions</term> <note>the traditional four temperaments: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic</note> nor the elements have anything to do. And note this as well: if such heat or cold were to come from the complexion, it would be possible for you to mutate the complexions as you pleased. If you could break a heat, you could create a cold, and conversely <note>original: "per contrarium"</note>. But it is just as in <term>putrefactions</term> <note>original: "Putrefactionibus," the process of decay or fermentation</note>—that is, a manure pile that lies together and is laid down cold; it has a nature within it that makes it become hotter than when it first came out of the horse's belly. And though it becomes ever so hot, it is still not an element, nor is it the "complexion" of the manure; it is a product of <term>digestion</term> <note>here meaning fermentation or internal chemical ripening</note>.

<margin>B</margin>All of this is merely a beginning of knowledge, leading to a greater understanding and a foundation for the theory of error and the process of open sores.

Note also that in Nature there are many such examples that might give "degrees" to a simple physician. Take <term>salts</term> <note>original: "Salibus"</note>, for example: they have a common element, but they accomplish nothing through that element. We cannot use or administer an element, for they are clear in their <term>virtues</term> <note>original: "Virtutibus," the specific healing powers or inherent properties of a substance</note>; they live from them alone and act from them alone. As for the further distinctions—such as <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "Salmiar"</note> compared to <term>sea salt</term> <note>original: "Sal maris"</note>, or <term>rock alum</term> <note>original: "Alumen rochum"</note> compared to <term>feather alum</term> <note>original: "Plumolum," likely a form of asbestos or fibrous alum</note>—this is not the fault of the elements. It is the fault of the Power, which is sour or sweet, sharp or salty; yet one has just as much of the element as the other. Therefore, <term>saltiness</term>, <term>bitterness</term>, <term>sweetness</term>, <term>harshness</term>, <term>roughness</term>, <term>sourness</term>, etc., should be attributed to that specific nature and not to other things; nor should one estimate a "complexion" to be higher or lower because of them. Such a nature is just as one human is distinguished from another by beauty or strength, which is not a property of the elements; likewise, the essence of <term>salts</term> <note>original: "Salia"</note> is a specific nature. Thus, <term>rock salt</term> <note>original: "Sal Gemmæ"</note> is sharper than <term>natron</term> <note>original: "Sal Anathron," an Egyptian salt/soda</note>, just as one human is sharper than another, and all of this is outside of the complexion. Just as one sharp tongue cuts more than another, yet they are all fleshy and of one form. And as rock salt is "prettier" than natron, it must also be more transparent and sharper. For beauty gives the <term>exaltation</term> <note>the refinement or heightening of a substance's properties</note> of the nature and virtue to the body, and not to the element. And as sal ammoniac is stronger than sea salt, that is the fault of "Strength," just as one man is stronger than another. Now look at where that strength comes from: for just as it is greater in one than in another, so also is the sharpness and piquancy greater in one than in another. The cold in <term>camphor</term> <note>original: "Gampffer"</note> is not of the element; it belongs to its specific nature, and it has not a speck more [of the element of water] than warm water does. Likewise, <term>Spanish flies</term> <note>original: "Cantharides," beetles used to create medicinal blisters</note> burn blisters, but not by the power of the element of Fire! For they have not a speck more of it than <term>chamomile</term> <note>original: "Camillen"</note> does. <term>Nettles</term> <note>original: "Nestlen"</note> also burn, not because of the element of Fire, but because of the subtlety of their form, which is their nature.

<margin>C</margin>These are <term>mysteries</term> <note>original: "Mysteria"</note> and <term>great works</term> <note>original: "Magnalia"</note> thus ordained by God above the elements and complexions. And whatever burns, bites, eats away, etc., is as closely attached to the "complexion" as a word is to the mouth [that speaks it]. For just as a word is not made of elements, neither are the nature and <term>natural virtues</term> <note>original: "virtutes naturalium"</note> of the elements. And if you undertake <term>philosophy</term> <note>here meaning the study of nature</note> with a correct foundation, your diseases will be seen to have a free origin, and not be like a <term>weaver’s pattern</term> <note>original: "Weberzettel," implying a rigid, predetermined structure</note>. Although you have not thought of such a foundation yourselves, it comes to you from those "philosophers" who should in no way be used in medicine with such errors and poorly-founded "doctoring." For <term>Aristotle</term>, <term>Averroes</term>, <term>Albertus</term>, and others will have no seat in such <term>natural sciences</term> <note>original: "Naturalibus"</note>, for they were not entrusted with medicine, so that they should be upheld with such authority. You know that the teachings of the philosophers and their like are set down in books without any experience, which should in no way have a place or position in medicine.

->Therefore I rightly say that the Philosopher should be born out of the Physician, and not the reverse. To prove this and bring it to light, let your own hands, arts, and faculties bear witness.<-

Likewise, fifthly, Doctor Matthias Unzerus, <term>Anatomia Spagirica</term> <gloss>Spagyric Anatomy</gloss>, Part 2, Chapter 17, page 124 and 126:

It is today placed beyond all controversy that iron, through a light artifice, through metamorphosis, can turn into true brass or copper. The people of Smolnitz know this above all, who every year change a great quantity of iron into copper, for which we provide the witnesses Werner, Matthesius, and others, who have contemplated such artificial copper with their own eyes and also recalled it to examination. That transmutation is carried out by vitriolic waters, by which the iron is corroded into a greenish pulp, which afterwards, by boiling, passes into copper, better than that which is smelted from its own vein. Aristotle reports in the island of Thaba, in the province of Tyrrhenia, that the ore of copper metal, after it was exhausted, offered nothing but iron. What other conclusion is there from this, than that the material principle of both metals <term>ψιλλίγεσθαι</term> <gloss>to be interchangeable</gloss>, and that it can sustain the forms of both, as it is formative. Since therefore the transmutation of the whole ore has occurred, why would the same not happen in a particle as well?

θείου ἡ διαμαρτυρηθεῖσα γνησία θυγάτηρ εἶναι. ἀλλ' οὐκ ἂν ἡ ἡμετέρα κατέστη μήτηρ. ἁλόντος δὲ τοῦ μάρτυρος, καὶ ἀποστάσης τῆς κλήρου τῶν ἀμφισβητούντων γνησίως θυγατέρα Πύρρῳ εἶναι, μεγάλη ἀνάγκη ἅμα καὶ τὴν τούτου μαρτυρίαν ἑαλωκέναι. ἢ γὰρ αὐτοῦ τούτου διαμαρτυρήσαντος τὴν δίκην ἐδικάζετο, πότερον ἐξ ἐγγυητῆς, ἢ ἐξ ἑταίρας ἡ ἀμφισβητοῦσα τοῦ κλήρου τῷ θείῳ γυναικός ἐστι· γινώσκετε δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ καὶ ὑμεῖς τῆς τε ἀντωμοσίας τῆς ἡμετέρας, καὶ τὰς τούτου μαρτυρίας. καὶ τῆς ἁλούσης διαμαρτυρίας. ἀναγίνωσκε λαβὼν τασδὶ αὐτοῖς.

<margin>Αντωμοσία. μαρτυρία. διαμαρτυρία.</margin>

Ὡς μὲν ἔδοξε παραχρῆμα εὐθὺς τότε τὰ ψευδῆ διαμαρτυρῆσαι Νικόδημος, ἐπιδέδεικται τότε πᾶσι. προσήκει δὲ καὶ παρ' ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐπ' αὐτῷ τούτῳ νῦν δίκην μέλλουσι ψηφιεῖσθαι, ἐξελεγχθῆναι πῶς τούτου μαρτυρίαν. ἐπιθυμῶ δὲ πρῶτον μὲν παρ' αὐτοῦ τούτου πυθέσθαι τίνα ποτὲ προῖκά φησιν ἐπιδούς. ἐκδοῦναι τὴν ἀδελφὴν ᾧ μεμαρτύρηκας, τῷ ἐν φιλτάτων οἴκων κεκτημένῳ. εἶτα πότερον κεγγύηται γυνὴ ἀπίλειπεν τὸν ἄνδρα ζῶντα ἢ τελευτήσαντος τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ· καὶ παρ' ὅτου ἐκομίσατο τὴν τῆς ἀδελφῆς προῖκα οὗτος. ἐπειδὴ τελευτηκὼς ἦν ᾧ μεμαρτύρηκεν οὗτος αὐτὴν ἐγγυῆσαι. ἢ εἰ μὴ ἐκομίζετο ὁποίαν δίκην ὑπὲρ τῆς προικός αὐτῆς ἐν εἴκοσιν ἔτεσι τοῖς ἔχοντι τὸν κλῆρον ἐδικάσατο· ἢ εἴ τιν' αὐτῶν οἵαν τίον προσῆλθεν ἐγκαλῶν τῷ κληρονόμῳ περὶ τῆς προικὸς τῆς ἀδελφῆς, οὐ χρόνῳ τοσούτῳ. περί τε οὖν τούτων ἡδέως ἂν πυθοίμην ὅ,τι ποτ' οὖν τὸ αἴτιον, ἢ μαθεῖν ὑπὸ γεγενῆσθαι ἢ τὴν ἐγγυητὴν ὡς μεμαρτύρηκεν οὗτος γυναικός. καὶ πρὸς τούτοις, εἴ τις ἄλλος ἐγγυητὴν ἔσχε τὴν τούτου ἀδελφοῦ γυναῖκα, ἢ ὧν πρότερον χρησαμένων, πρὶν γνῶναι τὸν ἡμέτερον θεῖον αὐτήν. ἢ ὅσοι ἐκείνου γιγνώσκοντος ἐπλησίαζον αὐτῇ, ἢ ὅσοι ὕστερον ἐπλησίαζον, τελευτηκότος ἐκείνου. δῆλον γὰρ ὅτι τὴν αὐτὴν τρόπον ὁ ἀδελφὸς αὐτὴν ἀποσι τοῖς πλησιάζουσιν ἐκδεδώκει. περὶ ὧν εἰ δόκειτε καθ' ἕκαστον διελθεῖν, οὐκ ἂν πάνυ μικρὸν ἔργον γένοιτο. ἐὰν μὲν οὖν ὑμεῖς κελεύητε ἢ ἐῶσιν, μνησθείην ἂν αὐτῶν. εἰ δὲ τισιν ὑμῶν ἀηδὲς ἀκούειν ἐστίν, ὥς τὸν ἐμοὶ λέγειν τί τῶν ζώντων, αὐταῖς ταῖς μαρτυρίαις ὑμῖν παρέξομαι, τὰς μαρτυρηθείσας ἐν τῇ προτέρᾳ δίκῃ. ὧν οὐδὲ μιᾷ ἐπισκήψασθαι ἠξίωσαν οὗτοι. καίτοι ὅπου κοινὴν αὐτὴν ὡμολογήκασιν εἶναι τῷ βουλομένῳ τὴν γυναῖκα, πῶς ἂν εἰκότως ἡ αὐτὴ γυνὴ ἐγγυητὴ δόξειεν εἶναι. ἀλλὰ μὴν ὅτι γε μὴ ἐσχημένοι εἰσὶ ταῖς περὶ αὐτῶν τούτου μαρτυρίαις, ὡμολογηκότες εἰσὶ ταῦτα. ἀκούσαντες δὲ καὶ ὑμεῖς αὐτῶν τῶν μαρτυριῶν γνώσεσθε, ὡς οὗτός τε περιφανῶς τὰ ψευδῆ μεμαρτύρηκε, καὶ ὀρθῶς καὶ κατὰ τοὺς νόμους οἱ δικάσαντες τὴν δίκην ἔγνωσαν, τὴν κληρονομίαν μὴ προσήκειν τῇ μὴ ὀρθῶς γεγενημένῃ γυναικί. ἀναγίνωσκε· σὺ δ' ἐπίλαβε τὸ ὕδωρ.

<margin>μαρτυρία.</margin>

Ὡς μὲν ἑταίρα ἦν τῷ βουλομένῳ, καὶ οὐ γυνὴ τοῦ ἡμετέρου θείου, μεθ' οὗ γε ἐγγυήσει, ἐκείνῳ μεμαρτύρηκεν, ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων οἰκείων καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν γειτόνων τῶν ἐκείνου, μεμαρτύρηται πρὸς ὑμᾶς. οἳ μάχας καὶ κώμους. καὶ ἀσέλγειαν πολλήν, ὁπότε ἡ τούτου ἀδελφὴ εἴη παρ' αὐτῷ, μεμαρτυρήκασι γίνεσθαι περὶ αὐτῆς. καίτοι οὐδήπου γε ἐπὶ γαμετὰς γυναῖκας, οὐδεὶς ἂν κωμάζειν τολμήσειεν. οὐδὲ αἱ γαμεταὶ γυναῖκες, ἔρχονται μετὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν ἐπὶ τὰ δεῖπνα. οὐδὲ συνδειπνεῖν ἀξιοῦσι μετὰ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων. καὶ ταῦτα μετὰ τῶν ἐπιτυχόντων. ἀλλὰ μὴν τῷ γε μεμαρτυρηκότι, οὐδ' ἐπισκήψασθαι οὗτοι ἠξίωσαν. καὶ ὡς ἀληθῆ λέγω, ἀναγίνωσκε πάλιν αὐτοῖς τὴν μαρτυρίαν.

<margin>μαρτυρία.</margin>

Ἀνάγνωθι δὴ καὶ τὰς τῶν πλησιασάντων αὐτῇ μαρτυρίας, ἵνα εἰδῶσιν ὅτι ἑταίρα τε ἦν τῷ βουλομένῳ. καὶ ὅτι ἐξ οὐδενὸς ἄλλου φαίνεται τεκοῦσα, ἀναγίνωσκε αὐτοῖς.

<margin>μαρτυρίαι.</margin>

Ὡς μὲν οὖν κοινὴ τῷ βουλομένῳ, ἣν οὗτος ἐγγυῆσαι τῷ ἡμετέρῳ θείῳ, μεμαρτύρηκε, μνημονεύειν χρὴ ὑφ' ὅσων ὑμῖν μεμαρτύρηται. καὶ ὅτι οὐδενὶ ἄλλῳ ἐγγυηθεῖσα, οὐδὲ συνοικήσασα φαίνεται. σκεψώμεθα δὲ καὶ ἂν αὐτῆς ὑπονοήσειεν ἐγγύην γενέσθαι τοιαύτης γυναικός. εἰ ἄρα καὶ τῷ ἡμετέρῳ θείῳ τοιοῦτόν τι συμβέβηκεν. ἤδη γάρ τινες νέοι ἄνθρωποι ἐπιθυμήσαντες τοιούτων γυναικῶν, καὶ ἀκρατῶς ἔχοντες αὐτῶν, ἐπείσθησαν ὑπ' ἀνοίας

uncle, the daughter who was testified to be legitimate would be the heir. But our mother would not have been established as such. If the witness is convicted, and the estate is taken away from those disputing that there is a legitimate daughter for Pyrrhus, there is a great necessity that this man's testimony be convicted as well. For the case was judged on his very testimony: whether the woman disputing the estate with my uncle was born from a wedded wife or from a courtesan. You yourselves know both our sworn statement and this man's testimonies, as well as the conviction of the false testimony. Take these and read them to the jury.

<margin>Sworn statement. Testimony. Conviction of false testimony.</margin>

It was shown to everyone then that Nicodemus decided to give false testimony immediately at that time. It is also fitting that his testimony be refuted before you, who are now about to vote on the penalty for this very thing. First, I desire to learn from him what dowry he says he gave when he gave his sister in marriage to the man you have testified to, who possessed an estate among the most beloved houses. Next, did the woman who was betrothed leave her husband while he was alive, or leave his house after he died? And from whom did this man recover his sister’s dowry, since the man he testified to have betrothed her to had died? Or if he did not recover it, what suit for that dowry did he bring against the one holding the estate during those twenty years? Or did he approach any of them to make a claim to the heir concerning his sister's dowry during such a long time? 

I would gladly learn the reason for these things: whether the marriage ever happened, or whether she was a betrothed woman as this man has testified. In addition to this, I would ask if anyone else had this man's sister as a betrothed wife, or who used her previously before our uncle knew her, or how many approached her while he knew her, or how many approached her later after he died. For it is clear that her brother gave her to those who approached her in the same manner. If it seems good to you to go through each of these points, it would not be a small task. If you command it or if they permit it, I might mention them. But if it is unpleasant for some of you to hear me speak of the living, I will provide you with the testimonies themselves, those testified in the previous trial, which these men did not even think to challenge. 

And yet, where they have admitted that the woman was common to anyone who wished, how could that same woman reasonably seem to be a betrothed wife? Furthermore, by the fact that they have not challenged the testimonies concerning these things, they have admitted these facts. When you have heard the testimonies themselves, you will know that this man has testified to obvious falsehoods, and that the judges who decided the case judged correctly and according to the laws that the inheritance does not belong to a woman not born from a proper marriage. Read, and you, stop the water <note>the water clock used to time speeches</note>.

<margin>Testimony.</margin>

That she was a courtesan for anyone who wished, and not the wife of our uncle, with whom he testified she was betrothed, has been testified to you by the other relatives and by his neighbors. They have testified to you that fights and revelry and much licentiousness took place concerning her whenever this man's sister was at his house. And yet, surely no one would dare to hold a revelry at the house of a wedded wife. Nor do wedded wives go to dinners with their husbands, nor do they think it right to dine with strangers, especially with any chance comers. Furthermore, these men did not even think to challenge the one who testified to this. To show that I speak the truth, read the testimony to them again.

<margin>Testimony.</margin>

Read also the testimonies of those who approached her, so that they may know both that she was a courtesan for anyone who wished and that she is not shown to have born children from any other man. Read them.

<margin>Testimonies.</margin>

You must remember by how many it has been testified to you that the one whom this man testified to have betrothed to our uncle was common to anyone who wished. And remember that she is not shown to have been betrothed to anyone else, nor to have lived as a wife. Let us consider if anyone would suspect a betrothal to have happened for such a woman, or if something of the sort happened to our uncle. In Thebes, the best and most notable citizens were in a state of factional strife against one another, as has been mentioned before. The leaders of one faction were <term>Ismenias</term>, <term>Antitheus</term>, and <term>Androcles</term>. knowing him to be young, and indeed his father <note>original: "τοῦ αὐτοῦ γε πατέρα"</note>, we saw nothing of the sort, by Zeus, at first, when we were in ignorance of these things <note>original: "ἐν ἀγνωσίᾳ"</note>. And before four days were completed, having suffered none of the terrors of the sea, we landed in the land which Minos, son of Zeus, adorned with good laws <note>original: "ἣν Μίνως Διὸς παῖς ἐκόσμει τῇ εὐνομίᾳ"</note>, having found the affairs of the city in total disorder, with evil war and a famine of Demeter <note>original: "ἀφορίαν τῆς Δήμητρος"</note>, that is, these very things happening, for which we had come <note>original: "οἷς δὴ, καὶ οὗ ἕνεκεν ἐγεγόνειμεν"</note>, we have lost. For there are not even more than four of those who attend my lectures, regarding the other things which have been recounted to us, and especially because they are accustomed to be trained in Roman matters; but those who are with us would barely suffice for the water we drink. Having fled one evil, therefore, we found a better one, to use the proverb, if indeed that one should be called an evil when compared to this. And if they happened to be with us, it would be a gift of Apollo <note>original: "Ἀπόλλωνος"</note> and great Zeus. But also Polydeuces with Alcinous <note>original: "Ἀλκινόῳ"</note>. There would be nothing preventing us from arriving at the compatible star, or perhaps even coming to the life of a woman. But these things did not accompany us without the gods, lest we should have enjoyed any of the external goods, and we would depart from here as quickly as possible <note>original: "τάχιστά τε ἐντεῦθεν ἀπίωμεν"</note> before seeing the sacred precinct of Zeus and greeting the statues of the other gods <note>original: "τῶν ἄλλων θεῶν ἀσπάσασθαι τὰ ἀγάλματα"</note>. <meta>The previous page's translation described a Neoplatonic or Christian ethical text regarding the soul and virtue. However, this page contains a passage from Aristotle’s Physics (Book III, Chapters 2-3). The transition marks a shift from ethical-theological concerns to fundamental natural philosophy, specifically the definition of motion and the relationship between the agent of change and the patient undergoing change.</meta>

# Physics, Book III

<margin>
<unclear>... because it is in the thing being moved ...</unclear>
</margin>

...upon the mover, so that to move is to exercise this activity upon the movable. <margin>note this</margin>
**A**nd for this reason, motion is the fulfillment <note>original: "entelecheia"; often translated as "actuality," it refers to the state of a thing having reached its full potential or functional end.</note> of the movable, insofar as it is movable. This happens through contact with the mover, so that the mover also undergoes an effect at the same time. The mover will always bring some form <note>original: "eidos"; the defining characteristic or "blueprint" of a thing.</note>, whether it be substance, quality, or quantity, which will be the principle and cause of the motion when it moves; for example, a man who is actually a man produces a man from what is potentially a man. And the puzzle is also clear: that motion is in the moved. For it is the fulfillment brought about by the mover itself. And the activity <note>original: "energeia"; the state of being "at work" or in operation.</note> of the mover is not something else; for there must be a fulfillment of both. For a thing is "capable of moving" by its potential, but it "moves" by its activity; yet it is active upon the moved, so that the activity of both is similarly one, just as the interval of one to two is the same as two to one, and the uphill is the same as the downhill. For these are one thing, though their definition <note>original: "logos"; here meaning the rational account or formula that explains what a thing is.</note> is not one. So it is also with the mover and the moved. <margin>the motion is in the thing being moved</margin>
This poses a logical puzzle: for it is necessary that there be some distinct activity for each. One is "acting" <note>original: "poiesis"; the process of making or doing.</note> and the other is "undergoing" <note>original: "pathesis"; the process of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>; the work and the end of the former is a "product," and of the latter an "affection." Since both are motions, if they are different, in what do they reside? For either both are in the one being acted upon and moved, or the acting is in the actor and the undergoing is in the sufferer (but if we must call this latter one "acting" as well, the term would be used equivocally). But if the acting is in the actor, motion will be in the mover—for the same reasoning applies to both mover and moved. Thus, either everything that moves will itself be moved, or it will possess motion without being moved. But if both are in the moved and the sufferer—both the acting and the undergoing—and teaching and learning, being two, are both in the learner, then first, the activity of each will not exist in each, and second, it is absurd for two motions to be moved at once. For what are these two alterations of the one thing toward one form? That is impossible.

<column-break/>

### Page 3

<margin>
<unclear>... it is not absurd for the activity of one to be in another ...</unclear>
</margin>

...but the activity will be one. Yet it is irrational for the activity of two things that differ in kind to be one and the same; and it will be so if teaching and learning are the same, as are acting and undergoing—to teach would be the same as to learn, and to act the same as to undergo, so that the teacher would necessarily have to learn everything, and the actor to suffer. Or is it neither absurd that the activity of one should be in another (for teaching is the activity of the person capable of teaching, yet it is *in* something, not cut off, but the activity *of* this person *in* that person); nor does anything prevent one activity from being the same for two, not in the sense that their "being" <note>original: "to einai"; the essential existence or essence of the thing.</note> is the same, but in the way the potential stands toward the active.
**T**he activity, as the genus of the underlying subject, is the same; like the interval from one to two and from two to one, or the uphill and the downhill road. For these are one, though the definition is not one. The same applies to the mover and the moved. How then is it not necessary for the teacher to learn, if acting and undergoing are the same? They are not the same in the sense that their definition of "what it is to be" <note>original: "to ti en einai"; Aristotle’s technical phrase for "essence."</note> is one, like "garment" and "cloak," but like the road from Thebes to Athens and the road from Athens to Thebes, as was said before. For not all the same things belong to everything that is in some way "the same," but only to those whose essence is the same. Moreover, even if teaching is the same as learning, "to learn" is not the same as "to teach"; just as, even if there is one distance between two separate things, "to be distant from here to there" is not one and the same as "to be distant from there to here." In general, neither teaching and learning nor acting and undergoing are the same in the strict sense, but that to which these belong—the motion—is the same. For to be the activity of *this* in *that*, and the activity of *that* by *this*, are different in definition.
We have now said what motion is, both generally and specifically. For it is not unclear how each of its types will be defined; for alteration <note>original: "alloiosis"; qualitative change.</note> is the fulfillment of the alterable, insofar as it is alterable. Still more clearly, it is the fulfillment of the potential to act and to be acted upon, insofar as they are such, both generally and again specifically, whether it be house-building or healing. Each of the other motions will be spoken of in the same way.
Since the science of nature is concerned with magnitudes, motion, and time, each of which must necessarily be either infinite or finite...

<summary>This page explores Aristotle's definition of motion as the "actuality of the potential," resolving the puzzle of whether motion resides in the mover or the moved by concluding it is a single activity shared by both, yet differing in definition.</summary>

> "The impossible, then, and the not impossible, follow the contingent, and the possible, and the non-contingent and the non-possible, contradictorily, but inversely. For the negation of the impossible follows the possible to be, <note>which is</note> the not impossible to be. And to the negation, the affirmation <note>follows</note>. For to the not possible to be, <note>there follows</note> the impossible to be. For the impossible to be is an affirmation. And the not impossible to be is a negation. And how the necessary stands, must be seen. But it is clear that it does not stand in this way. Rather, the opposites follow. But the contradictions are separate. For the not necessary to be is not the negation of the necessary not to be. For it is possible for both to be true of the same thing. For the necessary not to be <note>and</note> the not necessary to be."

Through these, he says that the propositions of the impossible, both affirmative and negative, are set out accordingly, and are placed under the affirmative and negative propositions of the possible and the contingent, with the negations being drawn in a direct line with their own affirmations. And the entire simple contradiction of the impossible is placed under the simple contradictions of those. And the entire <note>contradiction</note> by transposition <note>is placed</note> under those by transposition. # On the 17th of the same month, the memory of our holy father Anthony the Great.

This great Anthony the Egyptian was a witness <note>in the sense of a confessor of faith</note> in the desert. Being rich in parents and having only a sister, he placed her in a convent. He distributed all his possessions to the poor and went off to the eremitic life. He defeated all the powers of the demons, for they never ceased to hate him because of his cunning and skills. With many fasts and sleeping on the ground, the blessed one did not give in, even when suffering. Because of this, he was deemed worthy of foreknowledge and many signs. He recognized the souls of both the righteous and the sinners, those being carried to heaven and those being carried down to Hades. He struggled for piety when Maximus and Maximinus were reigning. Many became his students and successors in his asceticism, including Athanasius the Great and Hilarion the Great of Thebes. Having lived for one hundred and fifty years, he fell asleep in peace, his body being guarded by two of his students.

translation:

Furthermore, the name of virtue, as well as that of vice, is not used simply, but in many ways. For example, virtue can be a <term>hexis</term> <gloss>disposition/state</gloss> or an <term>energeia</term> <gloss>actuality/action</gloss>. Again, it may be ethical or intellectual. Vice is the same. Moreover, it may be practical or theoretical. The temperate, the just, and the courageous man possess ethical virtues, while the prudent and the wise possess intellectual ones. Again, virtue may be directed toward oneself or toward another. For instance, temperance is directed toward oneself, while justice is directed toward another. For the just man acts justly toward others, whereas the temperate man acts toward himself. Again, virtue may reside in the passion or in the action. For instance, courage resides in the passion, while justice resides in the action. For the courageous man shows courage in the face of fear, while the just man acts justly in his deeds. Again, virtue may be a mean or an extreme. For instance, temperance is a mean, while courage is an extreme. For temperance is the mean between licentiousness and insensitivity, while courage is the extreme between cowardice and recklessness. Again, virtue may be natural or acquired. For instance, temperance may be natural, while justice is acquired. For the temperate person is temperate by nature, but the just person is so by acquisition. Again, virtue may reside in the reason, in the spirit, or in the desire. For instance, prudence resides in the reason, courage in the spirit, and temperance in the desire. For the prudent man thinks with his reason, the courageous man acts with his spirit, and the temperate man governs his desires. Again, virtue may be directed toward God or toward man. For instance, piety is toward God, while justice is toward man. For the pious man is pious toward God, and the just man acts justly toward man. Again, virtue may exist in life or in death. For instance, courage exists in life, while perseverance exists in death. For the courageous man acts in life, while the one who perseveres endures in death. Again, virtue may exist in wealth or in poverty. For instance, liberality exists in wealth, while self-sufficiency exists in poverty. For the liberal man acts liberally in wealth, while the self-sufficient man is content in poverty. Again, virtue may exist in glory or in obscurity. For instance, magnanimity exists in glory, while humility exists in obscurity. For the magnanimous man acts with magnanimity in glory, while the humble man acts with humility in obscurity. Again, virtue may exist in word or in deed. For instance, truth exists in word, while action exists in deed. For the truthful man speaks the truth, and the man of action performs the deed.

<summary>This page categorizes virtue into various types, such as ethical versus intellectual, and explains their manifestations in different aspects of life and action.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, vice, ethical, intellectual, temperance, justice, courage</keywords>

**3** **Taamatos**, daughter of Zoilos, from the same city, [declared] in the street. For as long as I remain alive, I shall have authority over my own property to do whatever I wish, to alter my will, and to **4** revoke <note>original: "ἀκύρωσιν." To render the document legally void or cancelled.</note> this testament. If I should pass away with this will [unchanged], I leave out of affection <note>original: "κατὰ φιλοστοργίαν." A common legal phrase in Greek wills indicating a gift made out of natural love and family feeling rather than a commercial transaction.</note> to Dionysios, son of Panechotes—who is the freedman <note>term: <term>freedman</term>. A former slave who has been legally granted his freedom but often remains in a social or legal relationship with his former master's family.</note> of Petosiris—and of his mother Ammonous, from the **5** same city, who is currently a minor, if he survives; but if not, to his offspring, the property belonging to me in the village of Kriethyris in the [... district], which is a **6** shared portion held with my father Psenosiris, son of Atreus and of his mother Spokis, consisting of a house and courtyard, with its entrances and exits, and whatever else I may **7** leave behind in any manner whatsoever. If it happens that Dionysios dies childless and intestate <note>term: <term>intestate</term>. To die without having made a valid will, meaning the property would normally revert to legal default heirs.</note>, the things coming to him from me shall be **8** passed to those who are my nearest kin. I leave nothing to anyone else. This will is valid.

*2nd hand* I, **Tastraton** <note>Note the variation in the name: called Taamatos in line 3 but Tastraton here in her signature.</note>, daughter of Psenosiris, son of Atreus, have made this will, and I leave after my death to Dionysios, son of **9** Panechotes, freedman of Petosiris and of his mother Ammonous, a minor, the common portion in **10** Kriethyris... of a house and courtyard, and all else I may leave. the part closest to the eye will appear lower, and the parallel sides will converge at a single point.

**THINGS** located near rivers are less evident in distant places than those that are remote from such rivers and marshes.

**AMONG** things of equal thickness, those that are closer to the eye will appear more sparse, and those more remote will appear denser.

**THE EYE** that has a larger pupil will see the object as a larger figure. This is demonstrated by looking at a celestial body <note>original: "corpo celeste"; likely referring to the sun or moon</note> through a tiny hole <term>spiracolo: a small aperture or pinhole</term> made with a needle in paper; because only a small part of its light can operate, that body seems to diminish in size by as much as the portion of light seeing it is lacking from its whole.

**THE AIR** that is thickened and interposed between the eye and the object renders the boundaries of that object uncertain and confused, and makes the object appear larger than it is. This happens because linear perspective <term>prospettiva lineare: the mathematical system of creating depth through converging lines</term> does not diminish the angle that carries its images to the eye, but the perspective of colors <term>prospettiva de' colori: also known as aerial perspective, where color and clarity change with distance</term> pushes and removes it to a greater distance than it actually is; thus, one removes it from the eye, and the other preserves its magnitude.

**WHEN** the sun is in the west, the falling mists thicken the air, and things not seen by the sun remain dark and confused, while those illuminated by the sun turn reddish and yellowish, according to how the sun appears on the horizon. Furthermore, the things illuminated by this light are very evident, especially the buildings and houses of cities and villas, because their shadows are dark; it seems that their clear appearance arises from confused and uncertain backgrounds, because everything is of one color unless it is seen by the sun.

**AN OBJECT** illuminated by the sun is also illuminated by the air, so that two shadows are created; of these, the one that has its central line pointing directly to the center of the sun will be darker. The central line of the primary and derivative light will always be aligned with the central line of the primary or derivative shadows. <note>Leonardo distinguishes between "primary" shadows on the object itself and "derivative" shadows cast onto other surfaces.</note>

**THE SUN** makes a beautiful spectacle when it is in the west, illuminating all the high buildings of cities and castles, and the tall trees of the countryside, tinting them with its color. Everything else from there downwards remains with little relief, because being illuminated only by the air, there is little difference between the shadows and the lights, and for this reason, they do not stand out much. Those things that rise highest among them are touched by the solar rays and, as has been said, are tinted in their color; therefore, you must take the color with which you make your sun, and mix it into whatever light color you use to illuminate those bodies.

Rien de plus simple cependant : la planche ou la herse qui abat les fillons, est tirée par les bœufs en même tems que la charrue : mais elle est placée à côté, & non derrière ; ainsi tandis que la charrue s'avance en creusant un profond fillon, la planche s'avance également de front, en abattant tous les petits fillons qui font sur son chemin, & couverts de semence.

<term>Lirare</term> aura donc deux sens, abattre les fillons, & tracer des raies dans un champ. Nos Dictionnaires Latins ne marquent pas le premier ; ils sont donc inexacts.

### AUGUR, *Augure.*

L’origine de ce mot, si intéressant pour les Romains, est encore totalement inconnue : on n'en a pas même donné une étymologie passable : on a bien vu à la vérité qu'il étoit composé, 1^o. du mot A V E, *Oiseau* ; mais la seconde Racine a été indéchiffrable pour les Latins eux-mêmes. S E R V I U S sur *Aen. V.* le dérivé de *gero*, porter ; I S I D O R E de *garrio*, gazouiller ; d'autres de *gustus*, goût ; O V I D E (*Fast. I.*) d'*augere*, augmenter. Mais l'on voit par le passage même, qu'il avoit moins en vue de donner une vraie étymologie de ce mot, que de flater Auguste.

V o s s i u s discute gravement toutes ces absurdités, & se décide enfin pour *gero*. L'on croit lire des discussions de Barbares, ou d'enfans, sur des objets où ils ne voyent goute : ils courent tous ici à des étymologies frivoles, laissant à côté d'eux la vérité belle & brillante. C'est de C U R O que vint A U G U R E : de *curo*, dont la signification propre est, *regarder, voir, observer*. A U - G U R signifie donc mot à mot celui qui observe les Oiseaux.

N’est-ce pas l’idée même du mot Augure ; ce nom qui sembloit fait par hazard n'est-il pas une peinture vive de l'idée qu'il fut destiné à représenter ? Telle est donc l'utilité des étymologies : elle donne de la vie aux cadavres ; elle rend l'étude des mots aussi intéressante, qu'elle est sans son secours rebutante & insipide.

<header>GENERAL PLAN</header>

<margin>a</margin> This has greatly perplexed the French Translator of the 18th Book of Pliny, as he struggled with this passage from VARRO, *On Agriculture, book I. chap. 29.*

> "Thirdly, when they plow after the seed has been cast, the oxen are said to **ridge** <note>original: "lirare"</note>; that is, with small boards added to the plowshare, they simultaneously cover the sown grain in ridges <note>original: "in porcis"</note> and furrow ditches so that the rainwater may drain away. One cannot visualize," says the Translator, "this mechanism. A board attached to a plow may well knock down the ridges and cover the seed; but how can it simultaneously dig a deep furrow for the drainage of water?"

Nothing is simpler, however: the board or the harrow that knocks down the ridges is pulled by the oxen at the same time as the plow, but it is placed to the side, and not behind. Thus, while the plow moves forward digging a deep furrow, the board also moves forward abreast of it, knocking down all the small ridges in its path which are covered with seed.

<term>Lirare</term> <note>The Latin verb for ridging or harrowing.</note> will therefore have two meanings: to knock down ridges, and to trace furrows in a field. Our Latin Dictionaries do not record the first; they are therefore inaccurate.

### AUGUR, *Augur.*

The origin of this word, so significant to the Romans, is still completely unknown: no one has even provided a passable etymology for it. It was correctly seen to be composed, 1st, of the word **BIRD** <note>original: "AVE"</note>; but the second Root has been indecipherable even for the Latins themselves. SERVIUS, in his commentary on *Aeneid V*, derives it from **to carry** <note>original: "gero"</note>; ISIDORE from **to chatter** <note>original: "garrio"</note>; others from **taste** <note>original: "gustus"</note>; OVID (*Fasti I*) from **to increase** <note>original: "augere"</note>. But one sees by the passage itself that he intended less to give a true etymology of the word than to flatter Augustus.

VOSSIUS <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a renowned Dutch classical scholar.</note> gravely discusses all these absurdities and finally decides in favor of **to carry** <note>original: "gero"</note>. One feels they are reading the discussions of Barbarians, or of children, regarding objects they cannot see at all. They all chase frivolous etymologies here, leaving the beautiful and brilliant truth by their side. It is from **TO WATCH/OBSERVE** <note>original: "CURO"</note> that **AUGUR** came: from **curo**, whose proper meaning is *to look, to see, to observe*. **AU-GUR** therefore signifies, word for word, *he who observes the Birds*.

Is this not the very idea of the word Augur? Is this name, which seemed made by chance, not a vivid depiction of the idea it was destined to represent? Such is the utility of etymologies: they give life to corpses; they make the study of words as interesting as it is, without their help, off-putting and insipid.

MY first care was to examine first the embouchure of wind Instruments, to understand well how one could draw sound from them, the parts that contributed to it, & how it could be modified.

You know, Gentlemen, that the embouchure of a Transverse Flute differs from that of other wind Instruments, such as the recorder, the flageolet, & the Organ Pipe, in that in the latter, the wind introduced into a narrow but determined hole strikes the particles of the Body of the Instrument that are found immediately below; namely, the Bizeau <note>original: "Bizeau" - the beveled edge or labium of an instrument</note>: & by the promptness of its return, & its reaction on the particles that surround it, it is forced to suffer a violent collision. Thus communicating its vibrations to all the particles of the wood of the Flute, which in their turn communicate them to all the surrounding exterior air, it produces in us the sensation of sound.

But the embouchure in the Transverse Flute is indeterminate, in that it consists in the emission of the wind through a more or less large opening formed by the moving apart or bringing together of the lips, their position more or less close to the hole of the Flute, or more or less advanced over the edge of this same hole.

All these differences, which I reduce to the number of four in the embouchure of the Transverse Flute, make it, in its Playing, susceptible to an infinity of refinements & perfections that other wind Instruments, whose embouchure is determined, do not have; which I shall show in the explanation that I will give below of these different Movements.

Perch'i guardau' a i lor et a miei passi
Compartendo la uista a quando a quando.

Gridauan alto, uirum non cognosco:
Indi ricominciauan l'hinno bassi.
Finitol' ancho gridauan, al bosco
Corse Diana, et Helice caccione,
Che di Venere haue sentito il tosco.
Indi a cantar tornauan: indi donne
Gridauan' et mariti, che fur casti
Come uirtute et matrimonio imponne.
Et questo modo credo che lor basti
Per tuttol tempo, che'l foco gli abruscia:
Con tal cura conuien et con tai pasti
Che la piaga da sezzo si ricuscia.

### XXVI.

Mentre che si per l'orlo uno innanz' altro
Ce n'andauamo' et spesso il buon maestro
Diceua, guarda, gioui ch'io ti scaltro;
Feriami'l sole in su l'homero destro;
Che gia raggiando tutto l'occidente
Mutaua in bianco aspetto di cilestro:
Et io facea co l'ombra piu rouente
Parer la fiamma: et pur a tanto inditio
Vidi molt' ombre andando poner mente.
Questa fu la cagion, che diede initio
Lor a parlar di me: et cominciarsi
A dir; colui non par corpo fittitio.

**A**nd I saw spirits walking through the flame:
Because I looked at their steps and mine
Sharing my sight from time to time.
After the end, which is made to that hymn,
They cried aloud, virum non cognosco <note>Latin: "I do not know a man" (Luke 1:34)</note>:
Then they began the hymn again softly.
Finished, they cried again, to the wood
Ran Diana, and chased Helice,
Who had felt the poison of Venus.
Then they returned to singing: then women
Cried, and husbands, who were chaste
As virtue and matrimony impose.
And this mode I believe suffices them
For all the time that the fire burns them:
With such care it must be, and with such diets
That the wound is finally closed.

### XXVI.

While we were thus going one after another along the edge
And often the good master
Said, look, let me make you wary;
The sun was striking me on the right shoulder;
For already by radiating it changed all the west
From blue to a white aspect:
And I made the flame appear more red
With my shadow: and even at such a sign
I saw many shades walking and paying attention.
This was the cause, which gave the beginning
To them to speak of me: and they began
To say; that one does not seem a fictitious body.

...for ten: in essence, I assign him a great gain. This was a testament to his prudence and innocence. **THEN** he departed poor and old. It is as if he says: I consumed my life near an ungrateful lord without reward; and it moves one to compassion for his age, because as Diogenes said: "Nothing is more miserable than a man who is old and poor." And **IF THE WORLD KNEW THE HEART**—which was continent, just, and a despiser of riches and ease, frank and unconquered while he went about begging for necessary food. **PIECE BY PIECE** <note>original: "a frusto a frusto"</note>. *Frusto* in Latin means "piece." Therefore, it denotes that begging where a whole loaf is not given, but only scraps. **MANY PRAISE HIM.** It is as if to say: for his manifest virtues, many praise him. But if they knew his hidden virtues, which were marvelous, they would praise him much more.

### CANTO THREE OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'O' containing a portrait of a figure in a landscape, possibly Dante or a saint.</image-desc> **H**osanna, holy God of hosts <note>original: "Osanna sanctus deus sabaoth"</note>,
shining from above with your brightness
upon the happy fires of these kingdoms <note>original: "malachoth"</note>.
Thus, turning to its own melody,
that substance was seen by me to sing,
upon whom a double light was layered.
And it and the others moved to their dance,
and like most rapid sparks,
they veiled themselves from me by sudden distance.
I was in doubt and said, "Tell her, tell her,"
within myself, "tell it to my lady,"
she who slakes my thirst with sweet drops.
But that reverence which bosses
all of me, even for "Be" and for "ice," <note>original: "Be" and "ice" are the first and last parts of the name Beatrice.</note>
bowed me down like a man who slumbers.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' with architectural and foliate motifs.</image-desc> This seventh canto <note>The commentator correctly identifies it as the seventh canto here, despite the header.</note> is that in which Beatrice resolves several doubts concerning human redemption. First, how the sin of the first man was punished in the death of Christ. Then, why this way of recovery pleased God more than another. And she adds why human souls are immortal. First, therefore, he shows that Justinian, after his speech, returned to his accustomed song, saying: **HOSANNA.** In Hebrew, this means "save." He says, therefore, "O holy God of hosts" <note>original: "sabaoth"</note>, that is, of the armies and the virtues, "save us." I say: **SHINING FROM ABOVE** <note>original: "super illustrans"</note>, illuminating from above; **HAPPY FIRES** <note>original: "felices ignes"</note>, the happy spirits; **OF THESE KINGDOMS** <note>original: "HORVM Malachoth"</note>, of these realms.
**THUS TURNING TO ITS OWN MELODY** <note>original: "rota," literally wheel or orb</note>, that is, to its circular motion, because just as the heavens assiduously revolve around God, so do the souls of the blessed. Some texts say "note," and then we would say "to his song."
**WAS SEEN BY ME** <note>original: "VISO Mi fu"</note>, that is, it appeared to me. **THAT SUBSTANCE**, that is, that spirit.
**IS DOUBLE-LAYERED** <note>original: "SADDVA"</note>: is duplicated. **AND IT AND THE OTHERS MOVED TO THEIR DANCE** shows that the souls of those spheres turn like the heavens with much circling; and that by such motion they distanced themselves from Dante. And he describes these spirits in the form of sparks which **VEILED THEMSELVES**, that is, they covered themselves from him by sudden distance. And the meaning is that they suddenly moved so far away that he could no longer see them. **I WAS IN DOUBT.** A doubt was born in me which persuaded me that I should say to Beatrice: "tell her," who slaked my thirst <note>original: "mi destasti," interpreted here as quenching thirst</note>, that is, removed my thirst with her **SWEET DROPS**, that is, droplets—namely,

---

fulfilled my desire with the truth. And he intends that he desired Beatrice—that is, Holy Theology—to show him what he desired to know. **BUT THE REVERENCE** that I bear for her—which is no other reverence than having regard not to fail in the honor that is duly owed. **WHICH BOSSES** <note>original: "CHE SINDonna"</note>: which makes itself mistress of all of me, that is, which has more power in me than anything else; **EVEN FOR "BE" AND FOR "ICE"**, that is, even for Beatrice, putting the first and last syllables; **BOWED ME DOWN**, took away my daring to lift my eyes and look at her: **LIKE A MAN WHO SLUMBERS**, that is, who falls asleep, who bows his head and does not raise it. The meaning is that my will was to search for the truth in the Holy Scriptures, but the reverence for those things which say: "Do not seek to know more than it is appropriate to know" <note>original: "Nolite sapere plusquam oportet sapere"</note> restrained me from asking; and the reverence I bore for her was only for Beatrice, that is, for herself, to denote that the love and reverence one bears for sacred letters should not be to acquire honor or treasure, but for the sake of knowing, as has been said.

---

Beatrice did not leave me thus for long,
and began, beaming upon me with a smile
such as would make a man happy even in the fire:
"According to my infallible judgment,
how a just vengeance was justly
punished, has set you in thought.
But I will quickly release your mind;
and you listen, for my words
will present you with a great doctrine."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'H' with foliage.</image-desc> **I**t happened that Beatrice knew his thought, although he did not manifest it. And for this reason, she **DID NOT LEAVE HIM THUS**, that is, she did not suffer him to remain so pensive. But she decided to clear up the doubt for him. And he feigns this because no doubt can come into the human mind that cannot be resolved and declared in the Holy Scriptures. Nor is it without cause that he shows she spoke to him with a **SMILE** which could make even one in the fire happy: because nothing gives greater joy and pleasure to the mind than the knowledge of divine things, which content and satisfy our soul so much that even in every adversity they make us live happily. **ACCORDING TO MY INFALLIBLE JUDGMENT**, according to my opinion which can never be deceived, because this alone is true doctrine. **YOU HAVE SET IN THOUGHT**, that is, you think and go about investigating how a **JUST VENGEANCE WAS PUNISHED JUSTLY**: that is, how the fault of our first parents was justly punished in Christ. And if it was punished justly, how

---

could the Jews be justly punished for that which had been justly done? The doubt does not seem small. For if the death of Christ was just for the sin of the first parents, the vengeance taken upon the Jews was unjust. And if the vengeance taken against the Jews was just, then the death of Christ was unjust.

"For not enduring a curb upon the power
that wills, for his own benefit, that man who was not born,
damning himself, damned all his progeny;
whereby the human species lay sick
down there for many centuries in great errors,
until it pleased the Word of God to descend."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'U' with foliage.</image-desc> **W**ishing to resolve the doubt, she first demonstrates the sin of the first parent, Adam, saying: **THE MAN WHO WAS NOT BORN**, that is, Adam, who was not born from a mother's womb, nor was generated from paternal seed, but was formed from the mud of the earth by God. Adam, therefore, **DAMNED HIMSELF** by not enduring a curb. **UPON THE POWER THAT WILLS A CURB**, that is, upon concupiscence which requires a curb. **ALL FOR HIS OWN BENEFIT**, that is, for his own utility.
**HIS PROGENY**, that is, his lineage, namely all those who descended from him. **WHEREBY**: by which thing the human species **LAY SICK. That things indeed did not go smoothly for the Majapahit forces on that campaign is also apparent from the Kidung Sunda fragment mentioned above. As already noted above in Chapter I, this version presumably belongs to the oldest historical traditions, so the information certainly deserves attention. It is told there (cf. above, Chapter III) that the Sundanese <term>patih</term> <gloss>chief minister</gloss> Anepakĕn, in his dispute with Gajah-Mada, demanded that Sunda be treated as an independent kingdom based on recent events. <margin>How they anchored there,</margin>
On the 2nd ditto, we sailed 4 miles west and south-west. We had the island 8 or 9 miles to the west of us, and the wind was south-east. Thus, we sailed back and forth toward the east side of the island for almost the entire night, and made headway in the morning toward the north side of the island. Around noon, we came to anchor in the roadstead of St. Helena. Our land-anchor lay in 17 fathoms of water, and our ship had 20 fathoms, on black and sandy ground. We had a point to the north-east of us, and to the north-east by east a pointed mountain, not unlike a sugar loaf, on whose top stood a cross. The church stands in a hollow on the south-east side. In that hollow, and on the high land to the south-east of the church, as well as in the plain there to the side, it is full of trees. The other point of the land lay south-west by west of us.

<margin>And recovered the ship Hector.</margin>
On the third day following, we caught sight of the ship *Hector* again at night, coming to the south side of the island. However, it could not reach the roadstead, though it set its course as far toward the north side as it could with an easterly wind. On the 4th and 5th ditto, our boats went out to help it reach the roadstead, but they could not. On the 6th, as there was little wind, we did our best to tow it in, through which it came to 35 fathoms of water, one and a half miles from land, and about 2 hours from us to the south-west by west.

<margin>Departure,</margin>
On the 11th ditto, we set sail from St. Helena with an east-north-east wind, and set our course north-west. The north-western end of this island lies at the latitude of 16 degrees, with 7 degrees and 45 minutes of variation. ## CAPUT QUADRAGESIMUM SECUNDUM.
### Adulterina. Daun falawar.

**D**aun falawar Conyzæ quoque adfinis videtur, modo autem crefcendi convenit cum Nicotiana anguftifolia. Instar fruticis excrefcit ſtipite lignoſo, fex octove pedes alta, feſeque dividit in plurimos rotundos, & firmos laterales ramos, aliquando quam lattiſſime extenſos inftar arbustulæ.
Folia ſolitaria ſunt, & ſuperius compacta, longiuſculis inſidentia petiolis, anguſtifoliæ Nicotianæ ſimilia, ſed minora, ab utraque parte acuminata, oris æqualibus, ſeptem & novem pollices longa, quatuor & quinque lata, ſed ſuperiora in vetuſtis ſtipitibus minora ſunt, ſuperne intenſe virentia, ſed non ſplendentia, inferne cinerea, ad tactum rugoſa, ac præterea viſcoſa quaſi arena conſperſa, qualis & tota herba eft, ſi quæ conterantur, gravem ſpirant odorem fere inſtar fructus Bate, qui fœtet, ſapor non admodum acris eft, licet ſit amarus & penetrans.
Superiores caules multa gerunt capitula obſcure virentia & arenoſa, in umbellam quaſi collecta, quæ ſeſe aperiunt in floſculos ſordide albicantes, qui inſident calici barbato, & conſtant ex viridi piſtillo, & petalis quinque primo erectis, dein retroflexis cum ſtaminibus brevibus antheras flavas gerentibus, poſt illos fructus excrefcunt rotundi, globulos fclopeti manualis ſeu minoris referentes, arenoſi quoque, primo virides, dein flaveſcentes, intusque repleti granulis planis, in ſuccoſa medulla reconditis.
Folia peculiarem habent characterem, ſed potiſſimum vetuſtiora, quod una nempe ipſorum dimidia pars ad petiolum longior ſit altera. Radix ample diſperſa eft & lignoſa.
*Nomen.* Latine Adulterina, ſive *Folium zelotypiæ*, vel proprie Remedium contra noxam adulterii; Malaice *Daun ſalawar* eadem ſignificatione, Amboinice *Ayloun puti*. *Salawar* autem vocant Malaienſes vitium, quod pueris ſeu infantibus ſupervenit, quum unus parentum, ac præſertim pater adulterii ſit reus, ſeu uxori ſuſpicionem ejus criminis præbet, unde mater ſuſpica & iracunda lac ſuum adulterat, & illud infanti exhibens, ut puto, inde damnum contrahit, mulierculæ enim ſibi perſuadent, infectionem parentis apud alias mulieres contractam, lactantibus ſupervenire, unde hi emaciantur & languent, non autem viris perſuadent, ſimilia vitia ab ipſis peracta infantibus ſuis eſſe noxia.
Nonne hæc juſta est fides, ſeu potius credulitas, quam ſine dubio puto ortam eſſe a quodam genio *Salambar* dicto, quem Arabes & Æthiopes dicunt eſſe diabolum quendam, cujus officium eft ſolum, odium & ſuſpicionem excitare & cauſſare inter nuptos. Qua autem ratione hoc melius peragere is potuit, quam mulierculis perſuadere, ſi infantes ipſarum forte emaciantur, tum parentem adulterii eſſe reum. Hinc rixæ & iræ moventur, unde mox petunt fagas, quæ infantem incantatione, & ſuffimigiis ab hac infectione liberant.
Atque hinc hæc Herba zelotypiæ vocari potest, & genius ſeu Diabolus iſte *Salambar*, dæmon zelotypiæ. Cæterum meliore jure hæc vocatur *Tabaco utan* ſeu *Nicotiana ſylveſtris*, quod nomen huic herbæ magis proprium eft præcedente quarta *Sombong* ſpecie.
*Locus.* Crefcit in gracilibus ſoliis, in locis incultis, in agris, & poſt ædes pagorum.
