<meta>This page marks the beginning of a new section, the Mātṛkānighaṇṭu, following the conclusion of the Bījanighaṇṭu on the previous page. While the previous section focused on complex seed-syllables, this section begins a systematic dictionary of the primary "Mother" letters (the Sanskrit alphabet), mapping each vowel and consonant to specific deities and cosmic principles.</meta>

# Now Begins the Lexicon of the Mother Letters
### (Mātṛkā-nighaṇṭu)

Having bowed to the Lord of Obstacles <note>original: "Śrī-Gaṇeśa"</note>, the Man-Lion incarnation <note>original: "Nṛsiṃha"</note>, the Goddess of Speech <note>original: "Bhāratī" or Saraswatī</note>, the Supreme Lord <note>original: "Īśvara"</note>, and Shiva, I shall speak this Lexicon of the Mother Letters for the understanding of those with the simple minds of children. || 1 ||

The Fixed One <note>original: "Dhruva"</note>, the Savior <note>original: "Tāra"</note>, the Triple <note>original: "Trivṛd"</note>, the Vast <note>original: "Brahma"</note>, the Beginning of the Vedas, the Immortal Star <note>original: "Tāraka-avyaya"</note>, the Sacred Hum <note>original: "Praṇava"</note>, the Triple-Measured <note>original: "Trimātra"</note>, the Light of the Syllable Om <note>original: "Oṃkāra-jyoti"</note>, and the First One—these are names for the sacred syllable Om. || 2 ||

The Fair-Necked One <note>original: "Śrīkaṇṭha"</note>, He Who Resides in the Hair and Neck, the Path of Return <note>original: "Nivṛtti"</note>, the First of Vowels—the **letter A** <note>original: "A-kāra"</note> is also celebrated as the Mother and the Wind. || 7 ||

The Lord of the Half, the Small Lamp <note>original: "Dīpikā"</note>, the Left Ear, the Slayer of the Demon Madhu <note>original: "Madhusūdana"</note>, Indra, the Primordial One, and the Six-Faced One <note>original: "Ṣaṇmukha"</note>—the **long letter Ū** is known by the name of Protection. || 8 ||

The Radiant One <note>original: "Rocikā"</note>, the Right Nostril, the Immortal Being, He Who Took Three Strides <note>original: "Trivikrama"</note>, the Mother of the Gods, and the Destroyer of Enemies—the **letter Ṛ** is remembered as the Burning Sun. || 9 ||

The Lord of Guests <note>original: "Atithīśa"</note>, the Dwarf Incarnation <note>original: "Vāmana"</note>, the Liberating One <note>original: "Mocikā"</note>, the Left Nostril, the Mother of the Demons, and the Knower of Fate—the **long letter Ṝ** is the Ender of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripurāntaka", a title of Shiva</note>. || 10 ||

<summary>This page introduces the Mātṛkānighaṇṭu, a Tantric dictionary that assigns esoteric names and divine identities to the vowels of the Sanskrit alphabet, mapping them to deities like Vishnu and Shiva as well as parts of the human body.</summary>

<keywords>Matrika, Sanskrit vowels, Om, Vishnu, Shiva, Tantric phonetics, Shrikanntha, Narayana, Trivikrama, ritual anatomy</keywords>

the part closest to the eye will appear lower, and the parallel sides will converge at a single point.

**THINGS** located near rivers are less evident in distant places than those that are remote from such rivers and marshes.

**AMONG** things of equal thickness, those that are closer to the eye will appear more sparse, and those more remote will appear denser.

**THE EYE** that has a larger pupil will see the object as a larger figure. This is demonstrated by looking at a celestial body <note>original: "corpo celeste"; likely referring to the sun or moon</note> through a tiny hole <term>spiracolo: a small aperture or pinhole</term> made with a needle in paper; because only a small part of its light can operate, that body seems to diminish in size by as much as the portion of light seeing it is lacking from its whole.

**THE AIR** that is thickened and interposed between the eye and the object renders the boundaries of that object uncertain and confused, and makes the object appear larger than it is. This happens because linear perspective <term>prospettiva lineare: the mathematical system of creating depth through converging lines</term> does not diminish the angle that carries its images to the eye, but the perspective of colors <term>prospettiva de' colori: also known as aerial perspective, where color and clarity change with distance</term> pushes and removes it to a greater distance than it actually is; thus, one removes it from the eye, and the other preserves its magnitude.

**WHEN** the sun is in the west, the falling mists thicken the air, and things not seen by the sun remain dark and confused, while those illuminated by the sun turn reddish and yellowish, according to how the sun appears on the horizon. Furthermore, the things illuminated by this light are very evident, especially the buildings and houses of cities and villas, because their shadows are dark; it seems that their clear appearance arises from confused and uncertain backgrounds, because everything is of one color unless it is seen by the sun.

**AN OBJECT** illuminated by the sun is also illuminated by the air, so that two shadows are created; of these, the one that has its central line pointing directly to the center of the sun will be darker. The central line of the primary and derivative light will always be aligned with the central line of the primary or derivative shadows. <note>Leonardo distinguishes between "primary" shadows on the object itself and "derivative" shadows cast onto other surfaces.</note>

**THE SUN** makes a beautiful spectacle when it is in the west, illuminating all the high buildings of cities and castles, and the tall trees of the countryside, tinting them with its color. Everything else from there downwards remains with little relief, because being illuminated only by the air, there is little difference between the shadows and the lights, and for this reason, they do not stand out much. Those things that rise highest among them are touched by the solar rays and, as has been said, are tinted in their color; therefore, you must take the color with which you make your sun, and mix it into whatever light color you use to illuminate those bodies.

كذلك تدبير الحق العالم ما دبره إلا به أو بصورته، فما دبره إلا به كتوقف الولد على إيجاد الوالد، والمسببات على أسبابها، والمشروطات على شروطها، والمعلولات على عللها، والمدلولات على أدلتها، والمحققان على حقائقها. وكل ذلك من العالم وهو تدبير الحق فيه. فما دبره إلا به. وأما قولنا أو بصورته، أعنى صورة العالم، فأعنى به الأسماء الحسنى والصفات العلى التي تسمى الحق بها واتصف بها. فما وصل إلينا اسم تسمى به إلا وجدنا معنى ذلك الاسم وروحه في العالم. فما دبر العالم أيضا إلا بصورة العالم.

<header>### Gem of Lofty Wisdom in the Word of Moses</header>

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to go out into the rain when it fell and uncover his head to it so that it would touch him. He would say: "It has newly come from its Lord." Look at this knowledge of God from this Prophet; how majestic, high, and clear it is! The rain subjugated the best of humanity because of its proximity to its Lord. It was like the Messenger to whom revelation descends. It called him through its state and essence, so he went out to it to receive the divine benefit it brought from his Lord. Had he not obtained a divine benefit from it touching him, he would not have gone out to it. This is the message of the water from which God made "every living thing" <note>Quran 21:30</note>. Understand this.

As for the wisdom of him being placed in the ark and cast into the river, the ark represents his <term>nasut</term> <gloss>human nature or physical body</gloss>. The river <note>original: "al-yamm"</note> represents the knowledge he obtained by means of this body. This includes what was given to him by the faculties of theoretical thought, the senses, and the imagination. None of these, nor their like, would exist for this human soul without the existence of this elemental body. 

When the soul entered this body and was commanded to manage and direct it, God made these faculties tools to reach what God intended for it in the management of this ark, within which lies the tranquility of the Lord. He was cast into the river so that he might obtain the various branches of knowledge through these faculties. Through this, He informed him that even though the spirit managing him is the king, it can only manage him through these faculties. He accompanied him with these powers existing in this human nature, which was expressed as the "ark" in the language of symbols and wisdom.

Similarly, the management of the Truth <note>original: "al-Haqq"</note> over the world is only done through the world, or through its image. He only manages it through itself, just as a child depends on the existence of a parent, effects depend on their causes, conditions on their prerequisites, results on their premises, and proofs on their evidence. All of this is part of the world, and it is the management of the Truth within it. He only manages it through it. 

When we say "or through its image," meaning the image of the world, I mean the Beautiful Names and Lofty Attributes by which the Truth named Himself and with which He is described. Every name by which He is called has a meaning and a spirit that we find within the world. Therefore, the world is also managed only through the image of the world.

For this reason, He said regarding the creation of Adam, who is the comprehensive program of the descriptions of the Divine Presence—which are the Essence, Attributes, and Acts: "God created Adam in His image." His image is nothing other than the Divine Presence. He placed within this noble summary, which is the Perfect Human <note>original: "al-Insan al-Kamil"</note>, all the divine names and the realities of everything that exists outside him in the great, separate world. He made him a spirit...

...it is possible. In such places, one can use the few to attack the many. Great forests and lush grasses are where one sets an **ambush**. Open plains and sprawling fields are where **cavalry** can support one another. Where vegetation and obstacles provide cover, **foot soldiers** can engage in combat. On the open outskirts where there is room to maneuver, allowing for both advance and retreat, one should use **long halberds** <term>Ji: a traditional Chinese polearm combining a spearhead with a side blade</term> to face the enemy.

When crossing water or spanning great distances, or when utilizing differences in elevation where the enemy cannot get close, one should use **long-range crossbows** to face them. Where rocky cliffs provide concealment and narrow paths wind and turn, one should use **swords and bucklers** to face the enemy. In marshes of reeds and rushes where the branches and leaves obscure the view, one should use **spears and iron-staves** <term>Ge and Ting: the Ge is a dagger-axe, while the Ting is an iron-pointed staff or short spear</term> to face the enemy. These are all dictated by the **natural character of the terrain**.

Someone asked: "Suppose within the stockades and camps, the three armies are already at rest. If the enemy takes advantage of a lapse to launch a sudden assault and attack, what should be done at such a moment?"

**Dong** <note>Referring to Xu Dong, the author of the *Tiger Seal Scripture* (Huqian Jing)</note> replied: "Station the brave in the front and hide the timid in the rear. In a moment of sudden crisis, if the timid are forcibly driven to the front, they will surely blunt your own momentum and break the edge of your elite forces. It is better to keep them concealed."

The questioner asked: "In such a moment, how can one find the time—"

One purifies this deliquium according to the art, and one draws from it a metallic salt and a metallic mineral mercurial spirit of the property and virtue of the others from before.

One can, in this manner, reduce all metals, minerals, and marcasites <note>Sulfide ores</note> into salt.

Remark that all the Ethereal Spirits—that is to say, the spirit that passes in droplets like spirit of wine, and which are drawn from metals, minerals, and marcasites, reduced into true metallic salt according to our precepts, then regenerated—are called by the sages "spirit of wine double," undressed upon their own corrosive body. Then they form a volatile saline body that they have named "philosophical sal ammoniac," which, being reduced into liquor, has been called ethereal volatile spirit, dissolved salt, *altaest*, hell-fire, circulated, dissolvent, and universal medicine, spirit or double mercury, which reduces all metals and minerals into green vitriol, or philosophical salt. This salt or vitriol, being nourished and satiated by its own spirit—that is to say, by this double liquor that formed it—becomes melting and fusible like wax. # Physics, Book III

<margin>
<unclear>... because it is in the thing being moved ...</unclear>
</margin>

...upon the mover, so that to move is to exercise this activity upon the movable. <margin>note this</margin>
**A**nd for this reason, motion is the fulfillment <note>original: "entelecheia"; often translated as "actuality," it refers to the state of a thing having reached its full potential or functional end.</note> of the movable, insofar as it is movable. This happens through contact with the mover, so that the mover also undergoes an effect at the same time. The mover will always bring some form <note>original: "eidos"; the defining characteristic or "blueprint" of a thing.</note>, whether it be substance, quality, or quantity, which will be the principle and cause of the motion when it moves; for example, a man who is actually a man produces a man from what is potentially a man. And the puzzle is also clear: that motion is in the moved. For it is the fulfillment brought about by the mover itself. And the activity <note>original: "energeia"; the state of being "at work" or in operation.</note> of the mover is not something else; for there must be a fulfillment of both. For a thing is "capable of moving" by its potential, but it "moves" by its activity; yet it is active upon the moved, so that the activity of both is similarly one, just as the interval of one to two is the same as two to one, and the uphill is the same as the downhill. For these are one thing, though their definition <note>original: "logos"; here meaning the rational account or formula that explains what a thing is.</note> is not one. So it is also with the mover and the moved. <margin>the motion is in the thing being moved</margin>
This poses a logical puzzle: for it is necessary that there be some distinct activity for each. One is "acting" <note>original: "poiesis"; the process of making or doing.</note> and the other is "undergoing" <note>original: "pathesis"; the process of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>; the work and the end of the former is a "product," and of the latter an "affection." Since both are motions, if they are different, in what do they reside? For either both are in the one being acted upon and moved, or the acting is in the actor and the undergoing is in the sufferer (but if we must call this latter one "acting" as well, the term would be used equivocally). But if the acting is in the actor, motion will be in the mover—for the same reasoning applies to both mover and moved. Thus, either everything that moves will itself be moved, or it will possess motion without being moved. But if both are in the moved and the sufferer—both the acting and the undergoing—and teaching and learning, being two, are both in the learner, then first, the activity of each will not exist in each, and second, it is absurd for two motions to be moved at once. For what are these two alterations of the one thing toward one form? That is impossible.

<column-break/>

### Page 3

<margin>
<unclear>... it is not absurd for the activity of one to be in another ...</unclear>
</margin>

...but the activity will be one. Yet it is irrational for the activity of two things that differ in kind to be one and the same; and it will be so if teaching and learning are the same, as are acting and undergoing—to teach would be the same as to learn, and to act the same as to undergo, so that the teacher would necessarily have to learn everything, and the actor to suffer. Or is it neither absurd that the activity of one should be in another (for teaching is the activity of the person capable of teaching, yet it is *in* something, not cut off, but the activity *of* this person *in* that person); nor does anything prevent one activity from being the same for two, not in the sense that their "being" <note>original: "to einai"; the essential existence or essence of the thing.</note> is the same, but in the way the potential stands toward the active.
**T**he activity, as the genus of the underlying subject, is the same; like the interval from one to two and from two to one, or the uphill and the downhill road. For these are one, though the definition is not one. The same applies to the mover and the moved. How then is it not necessary for the teacher to learn, if acting and undergoing are the same? They are not the same in the sense that their definition of "what it is to be" <note>original: "to ti en einai"; Aristotle’s technical phrase for "essence."</note> is one, like "garment" and "cloak," but like the road from Thebes to Athens and the road from Athens to Thebes, as was said before. For not all the same things belong to everything that is in some way "the same," but only to those whose essence is the same. Moreover, even if teaching is the same as learning, "to learn" is not the same as "to teach"; just as, even if there is one distance between two separate things, "to be distant from here to there" is not one and the same as "to be distant from there to here." In general, neither teaching and learning nor acting and undergoing are the same in the strict sense, but that to which these belong—the motion—is the same. For to be the activity of *this* in *that*, and the activity of *that* by *this*, are different in definition.
We have now said what motion is, both generally and specifically. For it is not unclear how each of its types will be defined; for alteration <note>original: "alloiosis"; qualitative change.</note> is the fulfillment of the alterable, insofar as it is alterable. Still more clearly, it is the fulfillment of the potential to act and to be acted upon, insofar as they are such, both generally and again specifically, whether it be house-building or healing. Each of the other motions will be spoken of in the same way.
Since the science of nature is concerned with magnitudes, motion, and time, each of which must necessarily be either infinite or finite...

<summary>This page explores Aristotle's definition of motion as the "actuality of the potential," resolving the puzzle of whether motion resides in the mover or the moved by concluding it is a single activity shared by both, yet differing in definition.</summary>

<term>Semuntia</term> <gloss>half-ounce</gloss>: which is written thus: S. It is called <term>semuntia</term>, as if half of an <term>uncia</term>. For it consists of twelve <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Duella</term> <gloss>two-thirds of an uncia</gloss>: which is written thus: ƱƱ. It is called <term>duella</term>, as if two <term>sextulae</term>. For it consists of eight <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Sicilicus</term> <gloss>quarter-ounce</gloss>: which is written thus: Ɔ. It consists of six <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Sextula</term> <gloss>sixth of an ounce</gloss>: which is written thus: Ʋ. It is called <term>sextula</term>, as if the sixth of an <term>uncia</term>. For it consists of four <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Dragma</term> <gloss>drachma</gloss>: which is written thus: <note>A cross or X with a horizontal bar through the center</note>. It consists of three <term>scripuli</term>.

<term>Scripulum</term> <gloss>scruple</gloss>: which is written thus: ſſ. It consists of eight <term>calculi</term> <gloss>pebbles/smallest units</gloss> or six <term>siliquae</term> <gloss>carob seeds</gloss>. The <term>scripulum</term> is named after a diminution, from a small stone which is called a <term>scrupulus</term>. 

<term>Obolus</term> <gloss>half-scruple</gloss>: which is written thus: —. It consists of four <term>calculi</term> or three <term>siliquae</term>. 

<term>Cerates</term> <gloss>a small weight/carat</gloss>: which is written thus: Z. It consists of two <term>calculi</term>, or a <term>siliqua</term> and a half. 

<term>Calculus</term> <gloss>pebble</gloss>: which is written thus: 𐆑. It is the smallest part of a weight. It is called a <term>calculus</term> because it is as small as a pebble, which is trodden upon without bother. 

If, therefore, you divide anything into twelve parts and take away the twelfth, you will call it an <term>uncia</term>, and the remainder a <term>deunx</term> <gloss>eleven-twelfths</gloss>. If into six, a sixth is a <term>sextans</term>, and you will call the remaining five a <term>dextans</term> <gloss>five-sixths</gloss>. If into four, the fourth part is a <term>quadrans</term>, and the remaining three will be judged by the name of <term>dodrans</term> <gloss>three-quarters</gloss>. If into three, the third is a <term>triens</term>, and you will call the remainder a <term>bes</term> <gloss>two-thirds</gloss>. But if you take five from twelve, you will call the seven remaining a <term>septunx</term> <gloss>seven-twelfths</gloss>; and if five are removed, you will call it a <term>quincunx</term> <gloss>five-twelfths</gloss>. If, however, you divide it into two, both halves are called a <term>semis</term>. The rest can be equally learned and taught by the inspection of the calculation itself, through a certain art of words among those who converse, as much as by the stylus of those who write. But since I have premised something concerning the names and figures of the <term>unciae</term> and fractions, I shall now append how many <term>scripuli</term> accrue to the <term>unciae</term>.

( तीसरा हेतु ) अपनी जातिमें अवस्थित रहनेसे भी ( द्रव्य ) प्रधान है जैसे जो पार्थिव द्रव्य है वह सर्व अवस्थामें पार्थिवही रहता है अन्यभावको प्राप्त नहीं होता ( अर्थात् जो पार्थिव द्रव्य है वह पार्थिव ही रहता है और कभी आप्य, तैजस आदि नहीं होता ) इसी प्रकार शेष आप्य, तैजस, वायवीय और नाभस आदिको जानना कि ये भी अपनी २ जातिसे पृथक् नहीं होते ॥ ३ ॥ ( चौथा हेतु ) पांचों इन्द्रियोंद्वारा ग्रहण होनेसे भी ( द्रव्यही ) प्रधान है क्यों कि द्रव्यही पांचों इंद्रियों ( श्रोत्र, त्वचा, नेत्र, जिह्वा और घ्राण ) इनसे ग्रहण किया जा सकता है । और, रसादिक पांचों इंद्रियोंसे ग्रहण नहीं किये जा सकते ( केवल एक रसना इंद्रियसे रसका ग्रहण होता है इत्यादि ) ॥ ४ ॥ ( पांचवां हेतु ) द्रव्य सर्व रसादिक आश्रय स्थान होनेसे भी ( द्रव्य ) प्रधान है कि द्रव्य स्वतंत्र है और रस गुण वीर्य विपाकादि सर्व द्रव्यके आश्रयभूत ( अधीन ) हैं ॥ ५ ॥

"आरंभसामर्थ्याच्च" द्रव्याश्रित आरंभ यथा विदारिगंधादिकमाहृत्य संक्षुद्य विपचेदित्येवमादिषु न रसादिष्वारंभैः ॥ ६ ॥
"शास्त्रप्रामाण्याच्च" शास्त्रे हि द्रव्यं प्रधानमुपदेशे हि योगानां यथा मातुलुंगाग्निमंथौ चेति न रसाद्य उपदिश्यंते ॥ ७ ॥

( छठा हेतु ) द्रव्यमें आरम्भका सामर्थ्य होनेसे भी ( द्रव्य ) प्रधान है क्योंकि क्रियाका आरंभ द्रव्यके आश्रय ( अर्थात् अधीन ) है । जैसे विदारीगंधा ( शालपर्णी ) आदिको लाकर कूटे और फिर पकावे इत्यादि सर्व क्रियाओंका आरंभ द्रव्यमेंही होता है रसादिकमें किसी क्रियाकाभी आरम्भ नहीं हो सकता ॥ ६ ॥ ( सातवां हेतु ) शास्त्रके प्रमाणोंसे भी ( द्रव्य ) प्रधान है क्यों कि शास्त्रमें भी द्रव्यही प्रधान माना गया है । जैसे योगों ( नुस्खों ) के उपदेशमें मातुलुंग ( नींबू ) तथा अग्निमंथ ( अरनी ) इत्यादि द्रव्योंहीका उपदेश किया गया है कुछ रसादिक उपदेश कहीं किसी योगमें प्राप्त नहीं किया ॥ ७ ॥

"क्रमापेक्षितत्वाच्च रसादीनां" रसादयो हि द्रव्यक्रममपेक्षंते तथा तरुणे तरुणाः संपूर्णे संपूर्णा इति ॥ ८ ॥ "एकदेशसाध्यत्वाच्च द्रव्याणाम्" एकदेशनापि व्याधयः साध्यंते यथा महावृक्षक्षीरेणेति तस्माद्रव्यं प्रधानम् ॥ ९ ॥

( आठवां हेतु ) रसादिकोंकी द्रव्योंमें क्रमापेक्षा होनेसे भी ( द्रव्य ) प्रधान है अर्थात् रसादि द्रव्यके क्रमकी अपेक्षा करते हुए रहते हैं । जैसे तरुण पदार्थमें

(Third reason): Because it remains in its own nature. For example, a terrestrial substance remains terrestrial in all conditions and does not change into something else. Similarly, understand that substances of water, fire, air, and ether also do not deviate from their own nature. 3. (Fourth reason): Because it is perceived by the five senses. The substance is perceived by the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose. Tastes and qualities cannot be perceived by all five senses. 4. (Fifth reason): Because the substance is the support. The substance is independent, whereas tastes, qualities, potencies, and post-digestive transformations all rely upon the substance. 5.

"Because of the capacity for action." Actions are rooted in the substance. For instance, collecting Vidārīgandhā, pounding it, and cooking it—all these actions are rooted in the substance, not in the tastes. 6. "Because of the authority of the scriptures." In the scriptures, the substance is considered primary. In the instructions for formulas, such as for the citron (<term>mātuluṅga</term>) and the <term>agnimantha</term>, the substances are taught, not just the tastes. 7.

"Because the tastes depend on the sequence of the substance." Tastes depend on the condition of the substance. For example, in a young substance, the tastes are young; in a mature one, they are mature. 8. "Because diseases can be cured by a part of the substance." Diseases can be cured even by a portion of the substance, such as the latex of the <term>mahāvṛkṣa</term> <gloss>spurge tree</gloss>. Thus, the substance is primary. 9.

The definition of a substance is that which possesses action and qualities and is the inherent cause. 10.
